chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Nellie, a cruising yawl, turned on her anchor, her sails never stirring, and came to rest. The incoming tide had reached its height, and the wind had almost died. Since we were heading downriver, we could only anchor there and wait for the tide to turn.

Before us the Thames opened towards the sea, seeming to begin a waterway that would never end. Far out, sky and sea were joined without a seam. Against that bright distance, the barges coming upstream on the tide appeared motionless, their tanned sails clustered in red, sharply pointed shapes, their varnished sprits catching the light. Haze lay along the low shores as they flattened away into the sea and disappeared. Above Gravesend the air was dark. Farther inland, that darkness seemed to thicken into a sorrowful gloom, hanging without movement over the largest, and the greatest, city in the world.

Our host and captain was the Director of Companies. The four of us watched his back with affection as he stood forward in the bows, looking out to sea. Nothing else on the entire river looked half so much at home on the water. He looked like a pilot, and to a sailor a pilot is trustworthiness in human form. It was hard to grasp that his work lay behind him, inside that brooding darkness, rather than out there in the bright estuary.

As I have said somewhere before, the sea formed a bond between us. It kept our hearts close through years spent apart, and made us patient with one another’s stories—even with one another’s beliefs. The Lawyer, the finest of old fellows, had earned the deck’s one cushion by his great age and many virtues, and lay on its only rug. The Accountant had already produced a box of dominoes and was playing at building things with the bones. Right aft, Marlow sat with his legs crossed, his back against the mizzen-mast. His cheeks were hollow, his skin yellow, his back straight; there was something ascetic about him. With his arms hanging down and the palms of his hands turned out, he looked like an idol. Once the director was satisfied that the anchor was holding firmly, he came aft and settled among us. We talked idly for a moment. Then the yacht fell silent. For some reason we never started our game of dominoes. We were in a reflective mood, capable of nothing but looking peacefully about us. The day was drawing to a close in a stillness of exquisite, tranquil light. The water shone calmly. The cloudless sky was an immense, kindly expanse of pure light. Even the mist over the Essex marshes looked like a luminous gauze, suspended from the wooded slopes inland and falling over the low shore in transparent folds. Only in the west, above the upper river, did the brooding darkness deepen from minute to minute, as though the approaching sun made it angry.

At last the sun’s unseen downward curve brought it close to the horizon. Its glowing white turned to a dull red that gave off neither rays nor warmth. It looked ready to go out without warning, killed by the touch of the gloom hanging there over the multitude of men.

At once the water changed, and the peace upon it lost some of its brightness but gained in depth. In the fading day the old river lay smooth across its broad reach. After centuries of service to the people settled on its banks, it spread out with the quiet dignity of a waterway leading to the farthest ends of the earth. We saw that ancient stream by the solemn light of lasting memories, rather than in the brief, vivid glow of a day that comes and goes for ever. For anyone who has, as people say, “followed the sea” with love and respect, nothing is easier than to summon the mighty spirit of the past along the lower Thames. The tide moves endlessly back and forth in its service, carrying memories of the men and ships it has taken home to rest or out to fight the sea. It had known and served every man the nation takes pride in, from Sir Francis Drake to Sir John Franklin: knights, all of them, with or without a title, the great wandering knights of the sea. It had carried all those ships whose names shine like jewels through the night of time. There was the _Golden Hind_, coming home with her round sides full of treasure, to receive a visit from the Queen’s Highness and so disappear from the immense tale; there were the _Erebus_ and _Terror_, sailing towards other conquests, never to return. The river had known both the ships and their men. From Deptford, Greenwich, and Erith they had sailed: adventurers and settlers; the ships of kings and of merchants on ’Change; captains and admirals; the shadowy “interlopers” trading in the East, and the appointed “generals” commanding East India fleets. Whether hunting gold or chasing glory, they had all gone down that stream with the sword, and often with the torch, carrying word of the power at home, carrying a spark of its sacred fire. What greatness had not drifted out on that river’s ebb towards the mystery of an unknown earth!... Men’s dreams, the seeds of commonwealths, the beginnings of empires.

The sun went down, dusk settled on the river, and lamps began to show along its banks. The Chapman light-house, standing on three legs on a mud-flat, cast a strong light. Ships’ lights travelled along the channel, a busy movement of lights passing upstream and downstream. Farther west, over the upper river, the monstrous city still left its ominous mark on the sky: a brooding darkness by day, a sinister glow beneath the stars.
“This place, too,” Marlow said abruptly, “was once one of the earth’s dark places.”

Of all of us, he alone still “followed the sea.” The most anyone could say against him was that he was untypical of his profession. He was a sailor, certainly, but also a wanderer; most sailors live what one might call a settled life. They think like people who stay at home. Their home, the ship, travels with them, as does their country, the sea. Ships are much alike, and the sea never changes. Against these unchanging surroundings, unfamiliar shores and unfamiliar faces, the vast, shifting life of the world, slide past them. What veils it is a mildly contemptuous ignorance, rather than a feeling of mystery. To a sailor, only the sea itself is mysterious: it governs his life and is as impossible to read as Destiny. As for everything else, when his work is done, a stroll or a drinking bout on shore is enough to reveal a whole continent’s secret to him. Usually he decides the secret was hardly worth discovering. Sailors’ stories are straightforward and simple: all their meaning fits inside the shell of a nut that has been cracked open. Marlow, though, was no ordinary sailor, except in his fondness for telling stories. For him an experience’s meaning lay outside it, surrounding the story, rather than inside it like a kernel. The story revealed that meaning only as a glow reveals a haze—like one of those misty rings sometimes made visible by the ghostly light of the moon.

No one found his remark at all unexpected. It was entirely like Marlow, and we received it without speaking. Nobody even bothered to grunt. After a while he went on, very slowly: “I was thinking of ancient times, when the Romans first arrived here, nineteen hundred years ago—just the other day.... Since then this river has sent light out into the world—you say Knights? Yes; but it is like fire racing across a plain, like lightning flashing through clouds. We live in that flickering light—may it last as long as the old earth keeps turning! Yet yesterday this place was dark. Imagine a man commanding a fine—what do you call them?—trireme in the Mediterranean, suddenly ordered north. He is hurried overland across the Gauls and given command of one of those vessels the legionaries used to build. They must have been an astonishingly practical lot: apparently they could turn out hundreds in a month or two, if we can trust what we read. Picture him here, at the world’s very edge: a lead-coloured sea, a smoke-coloured sky, a ship about as stiff as a concertina. And up this river he goes, carrying supplies, or orders, or whatever you please. Sand-banks, marshland, forests, savages; scarcely anything a civilized man could eat, and only Thames water to drink. No Falernian wine, no trips ashore. Now and then a military camp, lost in the wilderness like a needle in a bundle of hay. Cold, fog, storms, sickness, exile, and death—death lurking in the air, the water, the bush. They must have died like flies here. Oh yes, he did his job. Did it very well, no doubt, without giving it much thought—except perhaps afterwards, when he could boast of the things he had endured. They were men who could stand up to the darkness. Perhaps he kept his spirits up by watching for a chance of promotion to the fleet at Ravenna, some day, if he had useful friends in Rome and lived through the appalling climate. Or picture a respectable young citizen in his toga—too much gambling with dice, perhaps—coming here with a prefect, or a tax-gatherer, or even a trader, hoping to repair his fortunes. He lands in a swamp, marches through the woods, and reaches some inland post where he feels that savagery, sheer savagery, has shut him in. All that mysterious wilderness life moves around him, in the forest, in the jungles, in the hearts of wild men. No one can prepare him for those mysteries. He must live surrounded by what he cannot understand and finds hateful. Yet it fascinates him too, and that fascination begins to work on him. The fascination of the abomination—you understand. Imagine his growing regrets, his longing to get away, his helpless disgust, his surrender, his hatred.”
For a moment he stopped speaking.

“Remember,” he continued, bending one arm up at the elbow with the palm turned out. With his legs crossed before him, he looked like a Buddha delivering a sermon in European clothes, without a lotus-flower. “Remember, none of us would feel quite that way. Efficiency saves us—our dedication to efficiency. Those fellows, though, were not really much good. They were no colonists. Their administration, I suspect, amounted to squeezing people, and nothing more. They were conquerors; conquest needs only brute force. Having that is nothing to brag about, because your strength is merely the accident of other people’s weakness. They seized whatever they could simply because it was there to seize. It was violent robbery, murder on a vast and aggravated scale, carried out blindly—as is quite appropriate for men taking on a darkness. Conquering the earth generally means stealing it from people whose skin differs from ours or whose noses are a little flatter. Look at it closely enough and it is not a pretty business. Only the idea redeems it. An idea behind it: no sentimental pretence, but an idea, and a selfless faith in that idea. Something you can raise up, kneel before, and make sacrifices to....”

He stopped short. Little flames slid along the river: green, red, white, chasing one another, catching up, coming together, crossing, then drawing apart slowly or quickly. As the night deepened, the great city’s traffic kept moving on the river that never slept. We watched and waited patiently; until the incoming tide ended, there was nothing else to do. Only after a long silence, when he said uncertainly, “I suppose you remember that I once spent a little time as a fresh-water sailor,” did we understand what awaited us before the ebb began. We were going to hear another of Marlow’s experiences that led to no firm conclusion.

“I don’t mean to trouble you much with my own personal adventures,” he began. In saying so, he showed the failing of many storytellers, who so often appear not to know what their listeners most want to hear. “Still, to understand what it did to me, you need to know how I came to go there, what I saw, and how I travelled up that river to the place where I first met the poor fellow. It was as far as a vessel could go, and it was the point towards which everything in my experience had led. Somehow it seemed to cast a sort of light over everything around me, and into my thoughts. It was dark enough, too, and pitiful. Nothing extraordinary in it. Nothing very clear, either. No, not very clear. Yet it did seem to cast a sort of light.

“As you remember, I had just come back to London after a long spell in the Indian Ocean, the Pacific, the China Seas—a thorough dose of the East, six years or thereabouts. I was hanging about, interrupting your work and taking over your homes, as if heaven had sent me to civilize you. For a while that suited me beautifully. Eventually, though, I grew tired of doing nothing. I started looking for a ship, which must be the hardest work there is. But no ship would give me so much as a look. In time I grew tired of that game as well.

“As a boy, I was mad about maps. I could spend hours staring at South America, Africa, or Australia, lost in the splendours of exploration. Back then there were still plenty of blank spaces on the earth. Whenever a blank on the map seemed especially tempting—though they all did—I would press my finger on it and say, ‘When I grow up I will go there.’ I remember the North Pole was one of them. Well, I still haven’t been, and I won’t attempt it now. It has lost its glamour. There were other places scattered over both hemispheres. I have visited some of those, and... well, let’s leave that alone. But one remained that I longed to see: the largest, the blankest, you might say.

“By then, admittedly, it was no longer a blank. Since my childhood, rivers, lakes, and names had filled it in. It was no longer that delightfully mysterious emptiness, that white patch where a boy could dream of glory. It had turned into a place of darkness. Yet one river there, a tremendously large river visible on the map, looked like an enormous snake stretched out: its head in the sea, its body lying in great curves across a vast country, its tail vanishing deep inland. Looking at its map in a shop-window, I found myself fascinated, like a bird staring at a snake—a foolish little bird. Then it came back to me that a large concern, a trading Company, did business on that river. Dash it all! I thought. To trade on all that fresh water, they must have boats of some sort—steamboats! Why shouldn’t I try to command one? I walked on down Fleet Street, but the thought would not leave me. The snake had put me under its spell.
“You see, that Trading society was a Continental business. But quite a few of my relatives live on the Continent. They say life is cheap there, and not as unpleasant as it looks.

“I regret to admit that I started pestering them. That in itself was something new for me. Getting things through other people was not my habit, you know. I had always gone where I wanted by my own road, on my own legs. I would never have thought myself capable of this. But somehow, you see, I felt I had to get there, by hook or by crook. So I pestered them. The men replied, ‘My dear fellow,’ and took no action. Then—can you believe it?—I turned to the women. I, Charlie Marlow, put women to work finding me employment. Heavens! You see how the idea had taken hold of me. I had an aunt, a dear, eager soul. This is what she wrote: ‘It will be delightful. I am ready to do anything, anything for you. It is a glorious idea. I know the wife of a very high personage in the Administration, and also a man who has lots of influence with,’ etc. If I fancied becoming skipper of a river steamboat, she was prepared to make an immense fuss until I got the post.

“Naturally, I got the appointment, and very quickly too. Apparently the Company had heard that one of its captains had died in a fight with the natives. That opened the way for me and made me all the more impatient to leave. Many months later, when I tried to recover what remained of his body, I learned that the first dispute had been a misunderstanding over some hens. Two black hens, yes. The man was a Dane named Fresleven. Thinking he had somehow been cheated in the bargain, he had gone ashore and begun beating the village chief with a stick. It did not astonish me in the least to hear this alongside the assurance that Fresleven was the quietest, gentlest creature who ever went on two legs. No doubt he was. But he had already spent a couple of years out there working in the noble cause, you understand, and probably felt that at last he must do something to assert his self-respect. So he beat the old nigger without mercy. A large crowd of the man’s people watched, too stunned to act, until someone—I was told it was the chief’s son—could no longer bear the old man’s screams. In desperation he made a hesitant thrust at the white man with a spear. Naturally, it slipped between his shoulder-blades without much difficulty. The entire village then fled into the forest, expecting every sort of disaster. Meanwhile Fresleven’s steamer also made off in a terrible panic, commanded, I believe, by the engineer. After that, no one seemed much concerned about his remains until I arrived to take his place. I could not leave the matter there. But when I finally had the chance to meet my predecessor, the grass growing through his ribs was high enough to conceal the bones. Every one of them was still there. Nobody had touched the supernatural being after he fell. The village, too, lay empty. Its rotting huts, leaning this way and that inside collapsed enclosures, gaped with black openings. Certainly a disaster had come upon it. The inhabitants had disappeared. Blind terror had scattered men, women, and children into the bush, and none had come back. I cannot tell you what happened to the hens either. Presumably the cause of progress got those as well. In any event, that glorious affair secured me the appointment before I had properly begun to hope for it.

“I rushed about frantically making preparations. Within forty-eight hours I was crossing the Channel to present myself to my employers and put my name to the contract. A few hours later I reached a city that invariably reminds me of a whited sepulchre. Mere prejudice, no doubt. Finding the Company’s offices was easy. It was the town’s greatest concern; everyone I encountered could talk of nothing else. They intended to manage an empire overseas and earn endless money through trade.

“A cramped, empty street lay in deep shade. Tall houses, countless windows with venetian blinds, absolute silence, grass pushing up between the paving stones; grand carriage entrances on either side, enormous double doors standing weightily half-open. I slid through one of those gaps and climbed a swept, bare staircase, dry and barren as a desert. At the top I opened the first door I reached. Two women sat on chairs with straw seats, knitting black wool; one was stout, the other thin. The thin woman rose and advanced straight towards me, still knitting, her eyes lowered. Just as I was about to step aside, as one does for a sleepwalker, she stopped and raised her eyes. Her dress was as unadorned as an umbrella-cover. Without speaking she turned and led me into a waiting-room. I told her my name and examined the room. A pine deal table stood in the centre, plain chairs lined the walls, and at one end hung a large, glossy map covered in every colour of the rainbow. There was plenty of red—always welcome, because you know that actual work gets done there—a devil of a lot of blue, a little green, orange smudges, and a purple patch on the East Coast, marking the spot where the merry pioneers of progress drink their merry lager-beer. None of those places was my destination. I was heading for the yellow, right in the middle. The river was there too, fascinating, deadly, like a snake. Ough! A door swung open. A white-haired head appeared, looking secretarial but compassionate, and a thin forefinger summoned me into the sanctuary. Inside, the light was poor. A massive writing-desk crouched in the centre. From behind it emerged what struck me as pale plumpness wearing a frock-coat: the great man himself. About five feet six, I reckoned, with his hand on the controlling end of millions upon millions. I believe he shook my hand. He murmured indistinctly and found my French satisfactory. _Bon Voyage_.

“Some forty-five seconds later I was back in the waiting-room beside the compassionate secretary. Radiating sorrow and sympathy, he had me sign a paper. Among other promises, I think I agreed not to reveal any trade secrets. Well, I have no intention of revealing them.

“I was starting to feel a little uncomfortable. Such rituals are unfamiliar to me, you know, and something in the air felt ominous. It was as if I had been admitted to a conspiracy—I cannot say exactly—to something not quite proper. I was relieved to leave. In the outer room both women were knitting black wool at a frantic pace. New people kept arriving, and the younger woman walked to and fro to introduce them. The older one remained seated. Her flat fabric slippers rested on a foot-warmer, and a cat lay in her lap. She had some starched white contraption on her head and a wart on one cheek; silver-rimmed glasses perched at the end of her nose. She looked over them at me. The quick, indifferent calm of her glance disturbed me. Two young men, looking foolish and cheerful, were being led across, and she gave them the same swift look of unconcerned knowledge. She seemed to know everything about them—and about me. A strange uneasiness took hold of me. There was something uncanny, something fateful, about her. Later, far away out there, I often thought of those two women watching the entrance to Darkness, knitting their black wool as though for a warm funeral pall. One kept introducing people, introducing them endlessly to the unknown. The other examined the cheerful, foolish faces with her old, indifferent eyes. _Ave!_ Old woman knitting black wool. _Morituri te salutant_. Few of the people she looked at ever looked at her again. Not half of them; nothing like half.

“There was still the doctor to see. ‘A simple formality,’ the secretary assured me, as though he shared deeply in all my griefs. So a young fellow, his hat tilted over his left eyebrow, appeared from somewhere upstairs and took me out. Some clerk, I suppose; there must have been clerks employed there, although the building was as silent as a house in a city of the dead. He was untidy and indifferent, his jacket sleeves marked with ink. Beneath a chin like the toe of an old boot, he wore a broad, billowing cravat. We were a little early for the doctor, so I suggested getting a drink. At that he turned quite jovial. Over our vermouths he praised the Company’s business extravagantly. Presently I remarked in passing that I was surprised he did not go out there himself. Instantly he became cool and controlled. ‘I am not such a fool as I look, quoth Plato to his disciples,’ he pronounced with great solemnity. He emptied his glass with a determined air, and we stood up.

“The elderly doctor took my pulse, plainly occupied with some other thought. ‘Good, good for there,’ he muttered. Then, with a sudden eagerness, he asked permission to measure my head. Surprised, I agreed. He brought out an instrument like calipers, measured me from front to back and in every direction, and wrote everything down with care. He was a small, unshaven man, wearing slippers and a worn-out coat something like a gaberdine. I took him for a harmless idiot. ‘In the interests of science, I always ask to measure the crania of men going out there,’ he explained. ‘And when they return?’ I asked. ‘Oh, I never see them again,’ he replied. ‘Besides, you know, the changes occur inside.’ He smiled as though enjoying a private little joke. ‘So you are going there. Excellent. Interesting as well.’ He examined me closely and added another note. ‘Any history of madness in your family?’ he asked as casually as you please. This irritated me intensely. ‘Is that another question in the interests of science?’ Ignoring my annoyance, he said, ‘Science would find it interesting to observe individuals’ mental changes on the spot, but...’ ‘Are you an alienist—a doctor of mental illness?’ I cut in. That odd little man remained perfectly calm. ‘Every doctor ought to be, to some extent. I have a small theory, and you messieurs who go out there must help me establish it. This is my portion of the benefits my country will gain from owning so magnificent a dependency. I leave mere money to other people. Forgive my questions, but you are the first Englishman I have had the chance to observe...’ I quickly assured him that I was far from representative. ‘If I were typical,’ I said, ‘we would not be having this conversation.’ He laughed. ‘That is quite a profound remark, and probably a mistaken one. Take greater care to avoid irritation than exposure to the sun. _Adieu_. What is it you English say, eh? Good-bye. Ah! Good-bye. _Adieu_. Above everything else in the tropics, one must remain calm.’... He raised a forefinger in warning.... ‘_Du calme, du calme_.’

“One last duty remained: taking leave of my excellent aunt. She was in a state of triumph when I arrived. I drank a cup of tea—the last proper one I would have for a long time—and we sat by the fire talking quietly at length. The room had the comforting appearance of exactly what a lady’s drawing-room ought to be. As our conversation grew confidential, I realized that she had described me to the great dignitary’s wife, and heaven knows how many others, as someone unusually gifted and exceptional: a lucky find for the Company, a man you do not encounter every day. Good heavens! All I was going to command was a two-penny-half-penny river-steamboat with a penny whistle on it! Apparently, though, I was also one of the Workers—with a capital W, you understand. A sort of messenger of light, an apostle of the lesser kind. At that time an enormous amount of such nonsense was circulating in print and conversation. My excellent aunt lived right in the current of this humbug and had been swept away by it. She went on about ‘weaning those ignorant millions from their horrid ways,’ until, I assure you, I felt thoroughly uncomfortable. I dared to suggest that the Company’s purpose was to make a profit.

“‘You forget, dear Charlie, that the labourer is worthy of his hire,’ she replied cheerfully. How strangely women lose touch with the truth. The world they inhabit is their own invention; nothing like it has ever existed, or ever could. It is altogether too beautiful. If they tried to establish it, the whole thing would fall apart before the sun first went down. Some damned fact that men have lived with contentedly since creation would spring up and topple it all.

“Then she embraced me, instructed me to wear flannel and write regularly, and so forth, and I went away. Out in the street, for no reason I could identify, I suddenly felt oddly like an imposter. It was strange. Usually I could leave for anywhere in the world with twenty-four hours’ warning, giving it less thought than most men give to stepping across a street. Yet faced with this ordinary undertaking, I had a moment—not of hesitation, exactly, but of startled stillness. The nearest I can come to explaining it is this: for a second or two it seemed that my destination was the centre of the earth, rather than the centre of a continent.

“I sailed on a French steamer that stopped at every damned port they possessed along that coast. So far as I could discover, this was solely to put soldiers and customs officers ashore. I kept watching the coast. To watch land slide past a ship is to turn a riddle over in your mind. It presents itself to you smiling or frowning, welcoming, magnificent, petty, dull, or savage; always silent, yet seeming to whisper, ‘Come and find out.’ This coast had scarcely any features, as if it were still being formed, and wore an unchanging, grim expression. Along a blue sea, its glitter dulled by drifting mist, the edge of an immense jungle stretched far into the distance, straight as a line drawn with a ruler. Its green was almost black, and white surf fringed it. The sun burned fiercely. The land appeared to shine wetly and drip steam. Here and there, within the band of white surf, little greyish-white marks gathered, perhaps with a flag above them. These were settlements hundreds of years old, still mere pinheads against the untouched breadth behind them. On we thumped, then stopped and landed soldiers; on again, to land customs clerks who would collect duties in what looked like a God-forsaken wilderness, a tin shed and flag-pole lost somewhere inside it. Then we landed more soldiers, presumably to guard the customs clerks. I was told that some drowned in the surf. Whether they did or not seemed to concern no one very much. We simply threw them out there and kept going. Each day the shore looked exactly the same, as though we had stayed in one place. Yet we passed different trading stations with names such as Gran’ Bassam and Little Popo. Those names sounded as if they belonged in some grubby farce performed against an ominous backdrop. Doing nothing as a passenger, alone among men with whom I shared nothing, looking out at the sluggish, oily sea and the coast’s unvarying darkness, I felt held apart from what was real. I seemed caught in the net of a dreary, meaningless delusion. At times I could hear the surf, and its voice gave me real pleasure, like hearing a brother speak. Here was something natural, something with a reason and a meaning. Sometimes a boat from shore brought a brief encounter with reality. Black men paddled it. Even at a distance you could see the whites of their eyes gleaming. They called out and sang, sweat pouring down their bodies. Their faces looked like grotesque masks. Yet these fellows had bones and muscles, a fierce vitality, a tremendous energy in their movements, as natural and real as the surf breaking on their shore. Their presence needed no justification. It comforted me greatly to watch them. For a little while I would feel that I still belonged to a world of plain facts. It never lasted: something always appeared to frighten the feeling away. Once, I remember, we found a man-of-war at anchor off the coast, shelling the bush. There was not even a shed on shore. Apparently the French were fighting one of their wars in that neighbourhood. Her ensign hung slack as a rag. Long six-inch gun barrels protruded everywhere from her low hull. The greasy, slimy swell lifted and lowered her lazily, rocking her slender masts. There she sat in the empty vastness of earth and sky and water, inexplicably firing into a continent. One of the six-inch guns would go pop. A small flame flashed and died; a wisp of white smoke vanished; a tiny shell shrieked weakly. Nothing happened. Nothing could happen. There was something mad about the operation, something mournfully comic in the spectacle. That impression survived someone on board solemnly assuring me that a native camp—enemies, he called them!—lay hidden somewhere out of sight.

“We handed over her mail and sailed on. I heard that fever was killing three men a day aboard that solitary ship. There were further calls at places with ridiculous names. In their motionless, earthy air, like that of a catacomb heated too strongly, death and trade continued their merry dance. We travelled along the shapeless shore, where dangerous surf seemed Nature’s own attempt to repel intruders; we entered rivers and left them again, streams of death running through life. Their banks were decomposing into mud. Their waters, grown thick with slime, spread among twisted mangroves that seemed to writhe at us in the extremity of helpless despair. Our stops were never long enough for a distinct impression of any one place. But a vague, oppressive sense of wonder kept growing in me. It felt like a tiring pilgrimage through suggestions for nightmares.

“More than thirty days passed before the great river’s mouth came into view. We dropped anchor off the seat of government, but my own work lay about two hundred miles farther inland. As soon as I could arrange it, I set off towards a place thirty miles upstream.

“For that stretch I travelled on a small sea-going steamer. Its captain, a Swede, recognized a fellow sailor and asked me up to the bridge. He was young, thin, fair, and gloomy, with straight, lank hair and a dragging walk. Leaving the wretched little wharf, he jerked his head towards the shore in contempt. ‘Have you been staying there?’ he asked. I told him I had. ‘A fine crowd, these government fellows, aren’t they?’ His English was extremely precise, and bitter. ‘Strange what people will do for a few francs each month. I wonder what happens to that sort once they go upcountry.’ I said I expected to find out soon. ‘So-o-o!’ he exclaimed. He shuffled across the bridge, keeping a watchful eye ahead. ‘Don’t count on it,’ he went on. ‘Just the other day I brought up a man who hanged himself along the road. Another Swede.’ ‘Hanged himself! What in God’s name for?’ I cried. His careful watch continued. ‘Who can tell? Too much sun for him. Or perhaps too much of the country.’

“At length we came into an open stretch of river. A rocky cliff came into view, with heaps of disturbed earth along the bank, houses on the hill, and others roofed with iron scattered among the excavations or clinging to the slope. Above this inhabited wreckage hung the constant roar of the rapids farther up. Crowds of people, chiefly black and naked, moved like ants. A landing-stage jutted into the water. Every so often a fresh flare of sunlight drowned the whole scene in blinding glare. The Swede indicated three wooden buildings, like barracks, on the stony hillside. ‘That’s the Company station. I’ll have your luggage brought up. Four boxes, you said? Right. Good-bye.’

“I passed a boiler lying sunk in the grass and found a track up the hillside. It bent around boulders, and around a small railway-truck overturned with its wheels in the air. One wheel was missing. It seemed as dead as an animal’s carcass. Farther on lay more rotting machinery and a pile of rusted rails. On the left, a stand of trees offered shade, and dark forms appeared to move weakly beneath them. I blinked; the climb was steep. A horn sounded to my right, and the black people began running. A deep, muffled explosion shook the earth, smoke puffed from the cliff, and that was the end of it. The rock face looked unchanged. A railway was being built. The cliff did not obstruct anything, but this pointless blasting was the only work in progress.

“A faint metallic clink behind me made me look round. Six black men were struggling up the track in single file. Upright and slow, they balanced little baskets of earth on their heads; the clinking followed the rhythm of their steps. Black strips of cloth covered their loins, with short loose ends wagging behind like tails. Every rib showed. Their joints resembled knots tied in rope. Around each neck was an iron collar, and a chain linked them all, hanging in loops between the men and clinking as they walked. A further blast from the cliff suddenly brought back the warship I had seen shooting into a continent. The same threatening voice spoke here. Yet no possible use of the imagination could turn these men into enemies. Criminals was the word used for them. Like the exploding shells, the offended law had arrived among them from the sea as a mystery they could not solve. All those thin chests laboured for breath together. Their flaring nostrils trembled, while their eyes remained fixed blankly on the slope ahead. They went by within six inches of me, never looking at me, with the total, deathlike indifference of miserable savages. Behind this raw material came one of the reclaimed, a product of the new powers operating here. He sauntered dejectedly, gripping a rifle halfway along its length. His uniform jacket lacked a button. When he spotted a white man on the track, he smartly raised the gun to his shoulder. It was merely a sensible precaution: at a distance white men looked so alike that he could not know who I was. Reassurance came quickly. He grinned widely, white-toothed and roguish, glanced at his prisoners, and seemed to include me as a partner in his lofty responsibility. After all, I too belonged to the great cause behind these noble and just activities.

“I turned left and went downhill instead of continuing up. I meant to let the chained men disappear before I resumed the climb. You know I am not especially soft-hearted. I have had to deal blows and ward them off. The life I stumbled into has sometimes required me to resist and sometimes to attack—attacking is only another way of resisting—without calculating the price too closely. I have met the devil of violence, the devil of greed, and the devil of burning desire. But by all the stars! those were vigorous, powerful devils with red eyes, driving and ruling men—men, I tell you. Standing there on that slope, I sensed that this land’s dazzling sunshine would introduce me to a different devil: flabby, fraudulent, weak-eyed, a devil of greedy and merciless stupidity. Only months later, a thousand miles farther on, would I discover how slyly he could work as well. For a moment I stood horrified, as if someone had issued a warning. At last I went diagonally down the hill towards the trees I had noticed.

“I skirted a huge man-made pit dug into the slope. What it was for I could not begin to guess. Certainly it was neither a quarry nor a sandpit. It was simply a hole. Perhaps it had something to do with a charitable wish to keep the criminals occupied. I cannot say. Next I almost stepped into a narrow gully, scarcely more than a scratch across the hillside. Down inside it, I discovered, someone had thrown a quantity of drainage-pipes imported for the settlement. Every single pipe was broken. Pure, deliberate destruction. Eventually I reached the trees. I had only meant to wander into the shade briefly. Instead, as soon as I entered, I felt I had crossed into a dark circle of some Inferno. The rapids were close. Their ceaseless, steady, headlong rush filled the grove’s mournful stillness with a mysterious sound. No air moved there, no leaf stirred. It was as though the hurtling speed of the earth launched through space had suddenly become something one could hear.

“Among the trees, black figures crouched or lay or sat against the trunks, holding to the ground. In the faint light they were half revealed and half erased, their bodies expressing every posture of pain, desertion, and despair. Another charge exploded on the cliff, and a faint tremor passed through the earth beneath me. The work continued. The work! This was where some of those helping with it had come to die.

“It was unmistakable: they were slowly dying. No enemies, no criminals, nothing of this earth any longer—only black shadows of hunger and disease, lying indistinctly together in the greenish darkness. They had been brought from every hidden part of the coast, with all the legality of contracts for a fixed term. In alien surroundings, eating food they did not know, they grew ill, ceased to be useful, and were permitted to crawl off and rest. Those dying figures were as free as air, and almost as thin. I began to pick out the shine of eyes beneath the trees. Looking down, I found a face beside my hand. A black skeleton lay stretched out, one shoulder resting against a tree. Slowly its eyelids lifted. Enormous, hollow, empty eyes looked up at me. Something like a blind white gleam stirred deep in them and gradually faded. The man looked young, scarcely beyond boyhood, though with them, you know, it is difficult to judge. I could think of nothing except to give him one of the ship’s biscuits my good Swede had provided, which I carried in my pocket. His fingers slowly shut around it and stayed shut. He neither moved again nor looked again. A piece of white worsted was tied around his neck. Why? Where had he found it? Was it a badge, a decoration, a charm, an attempt to appease something? Did it have any thought behind it at all? That small white thread brought across the seas looked startling against his black neck.

“Beside that same tree sat two other bundles of sharp angles, their legs pulled up. One rested his chin on his knees and stared at nothing with a look so dreadful it was impossible to bear. His fellow phantom bowed its forehead as though exhausted beyond endurance. Everywhere around them lay others, collapsed into twisted positions, like figures in a painting of a massacre or a plague. As I watched in horror, one of them lifted himself onto hands and knees and crawled towards the river for a drink. He lapped water from his hand. Then he sat in the sunshine with his shins crossed before him. After a while his woolly head sank onto his breastbone.

“I had no further wish to linger in that shade and hurried towards the station. Near the buildings I encountered a white man so astonishingly well dressed that for an instant he seemed an apparition. There was a tall, stiffly starched collar, white cuffs, a pale alpaca jacket, snow-white trousers, a spotless tie, and shiny varnished boots. He wore no hat. His hair was parted, brushed, and oiled beneath a parasol lined in green, held in a large white hand. This extraordinary sight even had a penholder tucked behind one ear.

“I shook hands with the miracle. He told me he was the Company’s chief accountant and that the station handled all its bookkeeping. He had stepped outside briefly, he explained, ‘to get a breath of fresh air.’ With its suggestion of a settled life behind a desk, the phrase sounded wonderfully strange. I would never have brought him into this story except that he was the first person from whom I heard the name of the man bound so inseparably to my memories of that period. Besides, I respected him. Yes, his collars, his enormous cuffs, his carefully brushed hair commanded my respect. He certainly looked like a hairdresser’s display dummy. But here, amid the country’s widespread collapse of standards, he maintained his appearance. That took backbone. Those starched collars and dressed shirt-fronts were feats of will. He had been there almost three years. Later I could not resist asking how he managed to keep such linen. A faint blush appeared, and he answered modestly, ‘I’ve been teaching one of the native women about the station. It was difficult. She had a distaste for the work.’ Here, then, was a man who had actually achieved something. He was equally devoted to his account books, which were in faultless order.

“Every other part of the station was a jumble: the people’s minds, the objects, the buildings. Lines of dusty, splay-footed niggers came and went. Manufactured goods—shoddy cotton cloth, beads, brass-wire—flowed into the depths of darkness, while a valuable little trickle of ivory flowed back.

“Ten days I had to spend at that station. It felt endless. My quarters were a hut in the yard, but sometimes I escaped the disorder by going into the accountant’s office. Horizontal boards formed its walls, fitted so poorly that narrow shafts of sunlight striped him from neck to heels as he leaned over the tall desk. There was light enough without opening the large shutter. The room was hot as well. Huge flies buzzed like devils; their bites felt less like stings than stab wounds. I usually sat on the floor. Immaculate, even faintly perfumed, he perched on a high stool and kept writing, writing. Occasionally he got to his feet for exercise. When they installed a low truckle-bed containing a sick man, some agent brought down ill from upcountry, he showed a mild displeasure. ‘This sick person’s groaning interrupts my concentration,’ he said. ‘And even without it, preventing clerical mistakes is extremely difficult in this climate.’

“One day, still looking down, he observed, ‘You will certainly meet Mr. Kurtz in the interior.’ I asked who Mr. Kurtz was. A first-class agent, he told me. My disappointment with that answer made him put down his pen and add, slowly, ‘He is a very remarkable person.’ By asking more, I learned that Mr. Kurtz currently commanded a trading-post, an especially important one, deep in the real ivory-country, ‘the very bottom of there. Sends in as much ivory as all the others put together...’ He returned to his writing. The patient was now too sick even to groan. The flies hummed in a profound peace.

“All at once a murmur of voices began to swell, accompanied by the tramp of many feet. A caravan had arrived. Beyond the plank wall a fierce confusion of rough voices broke out. Every carrier was talking at once. Through the uproar came the chief agent’s wretched voice, tearfully ‘giving it up’ for perhaps the twentieth time that day.... The accountant got slowly to his feet. ‘What an appalling noise,’ he said. Quietly he crossed to the sick man, inspected him, and came back. ‘He cannot hear it,’ he told me. ‘What! Is he dead?’ I asked in alarm. ‘Not yet,’ he answered, quite undisturbed. He nodded towards the clamour in the yard. ‘When your work depends on making accurate entries, you grow to hate those savages. Hate them to the point of death.’ He considered this for a moment. ‘When you meet Mr. Kurtz,’ he continued, ‘give him my message: everything here’—his eyes went to the deck—‘is entirely satisfactory. I prefer not to write. With our messengers, one never knows who might read a letter at that Central Station.’ His gentle, protruding eyes stayed on me for a moment. ‘Oh, that man will advance a long way, a very long way,’ he resumed. ‘Soon he will be someone of consequence in the Administration. The people at the top—the Council in Europe, you understand—intend it.’

“He went back to his accounts. The disturbance outside had ended. A little later, as I left, I paused in the doorway. Through the flies’ steady drone I could see the agent bound for home lying spent and unconscious, while the other bent over the ledgers, accurately recording entirely proper transactions. Fifty feet below the threshold lay the motionless crowns of the trees in the grove of death.
“Finally, the following day I set out from that station with sixty men in a caravan, facing a walk of two hundred miles.

“There is little point in saying much about the journey. Tracks everywhere, tracks upon tracks, a network worn into the empty country: through high grass, burnt grass, tangled bushes, down and up cold ravines, over rocky hills blazing hot. And solitude, solitude; no person, not even a hut. The inhabitants had left long before. Well, suppose crowds of mysterious niggers with every kind of frightening weapon began marching between Deal and Gravesend, seizing country folk on all sides to carry burdens for them. I imagine the farms and cottages there would empty quickly enough. Here, though, even the houses had disappeared. We did pass several deserted villages. There is something sadly childlike about the remnants of walls made from grass. Day after day I heard sixty pairs of bare feet stamping and shuffling behind me, each pair carrying a sixty-pound load. Make camp, cook, sleep, break camp, walk. Sometimes a carrier had died in harness and lay at rest in the long grass beside the track, his empty water-gourd and long staff next to him. Above and around us, an immense silence. On a quiet night, perhaps, distant drums would tremble through it, fading and swelling, a vast, faint vibration. Strange, appealing, full of suggestion, wild; perhaps it held a meaning as deep as church bells do in a Christian land. Once we met a white man in an unbuttoned uniform, camped on the track with a guard of thin Zanzibaris carrying weapons. He was extremely hospitable and merry, to say nothing of drunk. He claimed to be supervising maintenance of the road. I could see neither a road nor any maintenance—unless one counts as a lasting improvement the body of a middle-aged negro with a bullet-hole in his forehead, which I literally tripped over three miles farther along. I too had a white companion. A decent enough fellow, but too fat, and given to the maddening habit of fainting on hot slopes miles from the smallest patch of shade or drop of water. Holding your coat over someone’s head like a parasol while he recovers is irritating, you know. Once I could not stop myself asking what he had come there for in the first place. ‘To make money, of course. What do you think?’ he replied contemptuously. Later he caught a fever, and we had to carry him in a hammock hanging from a pole. At sixteen stone he caused me endless quarrels with the carriers. They refused, deserted, slipped away at night with their loads. It amounted to a mutiny. One evening I addressed them in English, using gestures that none of the sixty pairs of watching eyes missed. Next morning I managed to send the hammock off ahead of me. An hour later I found the entire arrangement wrecked in a bush: man, hammock, blankets, groans, horrors. The weighty pole had scraped the skin off his poor nose. He badly wanted me to kill someone, but there was not a carrier anywhere in sight. I thought of the old doctor: ‘It would be interesting for science to watch the mental changes of individuals, on the spot.’ I seemed to be growing scientifically interesting. Still, none of this leads anywhere. On day fifteen I saw the great river once more and limped into the Central Station. It stood on a backwater amid scrub and forest. One side was prettily edged with stinking mud; the remaining three were bounded by a rickety fence of rushes. A neglected hole in the fence served as its gate. A single look told you that the flabby devil was in charge of this enterprise. White men holding long staffs drifted listlessly out of the buildings, wandered over to inspect me, then withdrew somewhere from view. As soon as I introduced myself, one of them, a stout, excitable man with black moustaches, began an elaborate, rambling explanation: my steamer lay at the river’s bottom. I was stunned. What? How? Why? Oh, it was ‘all right.’ The ‘manager himself’ had been present. Everything perfectly proper. ‘Everybody had behaved splendidly! splendidly!’ In his excitement he insisted, ‘You must see the general manager immediately. He is waiting!’

“At first I missed what that wreck really meant. I think I understand it now, though I cannot be certain—not in the least. Looking back, the business was certainly too stupid to seem entirely natural. And yet... At the time, though, it appeared to be nothing more than a damned inconvenience. My steamer had sunk. Two days earlier they had suddenly rushed off upriver with the manager aboard and some volunteer acting as captain. Within three hours they had ripped her bottom open on rocks, and she went down close to the south bank. With my boat gone, I wondered what use I could possibly be there. In fact, raising the vessel I was supposed to command gave me more than enough to do. I had to begin the very next morning. Recovering her, then repairing the pieces once I had brought them to the station, occupied several months.

“My first meeting with the manager was peculiar. Although I had walked twenty miles that morning, he never offered me a seat. His colouring, face, manner, and voice were all unremarkable. He was of average height and build. His eyes were an ordinary blue, though perhaps unusually cold; certainly he could bring a look down on you with the cutting weight of an axe. Even then, everything else about him seemed to deny any such intention. Otherwise his only distinction was a faint, elusive expression around the lips, something furtive. A smile—or not a smile. I remember it but cannot describe it. He did it unconsciously, though for an instant after speaking it would grow stronger. It closed each of his remarks like a seal pressed onto the words, making even a commonplace phrase seem impossible to interpret. He was simply a trader who had worked in those parts since he was young. Nothing more. People obeyed him, although he aroused neither affection nor fear, nor even respect. What he aroused was uneasiness. That was it! Uneasiness. Nothing so definite as distrust, just an unsettled feeling. You cannot imagine how useful that sort of... of... ability can be. Organization, initiative, even order: he had no gift for any of them. The station’s miserable condition made that obvious. He possessed neither education nor intelligence. Why had the position fallen to him? Perhaps because he never fell ill... He had completed three terms out there, each lasting three years... When everyone else’s constitution collapses, triumphant good health is a power of its own. During leave at home he indulged in riotous living on a grand, pompous scale. A sailor ashore—Jack ashore—with a difference only on the surface. That much emerged from his casual conversation. He started nothing; all he could do was keep the daily routine moving. Yet he was great. His greatness rested on this small fact: no one could tell what might restrain such a man. He never disclosed that secret. Perhaps there was nothing inside him. That suspicion brought you up short, because out there nothing external held anyone in check. Once, when assorted tropical illnesses had brought down nearly every ‘agent’ at the station, someone heard him remark, ‘Men who come out here should have no entrails.’ His smile sealed the remark as though closing a door onto a darkness he kept in his possession. You thought you had glimpsed something, but now the seal was shut. At meals the white men’s endless disputes over precedence irritated him. He ordered a huge round table made, so large that it needed a building of its own. That became the station’s mess-room. His seat was the place of honour; nobody else’s place counted. You felt certain he held that conviction immovably. He was neither polite nor rude, simply quiet. His ‘boy,’ an overfed young negro from the coast, was allowed to be outrageously insolent to the white men, right in front of him.

“The instant he saw me he started talking. I had taken a very long time on the road. He could wait no longer. He had been forced to leave without me. The stations upstream needed relief. Delays had mounted until he had no idea who was alive, who was dead, or how anyone was managing. On and on it went. He ignored my attempts to explain and fiddled with a stick of sealing-wax, repeatedly calling the situation ‘very grave, very grave.’ Rumour said an important station was in danger and its chief, Mr. Kurtz, had fallen ill. He hoped the report was false. Mr. Kurtz was... I was exhausted and irritable. To hell with Kurtz, I thought, and interrupted to say I had heard about him on the coast. ‘Ah! They speak of him down there, then,’ he murmured to himself. He resumed, telling me that Mr. Kurtz was his finest agent, an extraordinary man, indispensable to the Company. Surely I could appreciate his anxiety. He described himself as ‘very, very uneasy.’ He certainly shifted about a great deal in his chair. Exclaiming, ‘Ah, Mr. Kurtz!’ he snapped the sealing-wax and appeared astonished at what he had done. Next he wanted to ask ‘how long it would take to’... Again I cut him off. I was hungry, you see, and still being kept standing. My temper was growing savage. ‘How should I know?’ I said. ‘I have not even looked at the wreck. Several months, presumably.’ The entire discussion seemed useless. ‘Several months,’ he repeated. ‘Well, suppose we say three months before we can set off. Yes, that should settle the affair.’ I stormed out of his hut—he occupied a clay hut alone, with something like a verandah—muttering what I thought of him. A babbling fool. Later I withdrew that judgment when I came to realize, with a shock, the extraordinary precision with which he had calculated the time the ‘affair’ would require.

“The next morning I started work, with my back turned, so to speak, on the station. That seemed the only way to keep hold of the facts that redeem life. Still, you have to glance around occasionally. Whenever I did, there was the station and those men drifting without purpose through its sunlit yard. Sometimes I wondered what any of it meant. With their ridiculous long staffs, they roamed to and fro like faithless pilgrims held under a spell inside a decaying fence. ‘Ivory’ rang out everywhere, whispered and sighed. You would have thought it was the object of their prayers. A stench of stupid greed ran through everything, like a breath from a dead body. By Jove! Nothing I have ever seen has seemed so unreal. Beyond it all, the silent wilderness encircling that tiny clearing seemed immense and unconquerable, like evil or truth. It waited patiently for this fantastic invasion to pass away.

“Oh, those months! Well, leave that aside. There were various incidents. One evening a grass shed packed with calico, printed cotton, beads, and heaven knows what else erupted in flames. It happened so fast that you could imagine the earth splitting open to release a fire of vengeance upon all that rubbish. I was quietly smoking beside my steamer, which lay in pieces. In the blaze I saw everyone leaping about with raised arms. Down to the river rushed the stout man with moustaches, carrying a tin bucket. He assured me that everyone was ‘behaving splendidly, splendidly,’ scooped up roughly a quart of water, and raced back. The bottom of his bucket had a hole in it.

“I walked up slowly. There was no reason to hurry: the whole thing had flared like a box of matches. From the start, nothing could have saved it. Flames shot into the air, forced everyone back, illuminated the place, and fell in on themselves. Already the shed was a fiercely glowing mound of embers. Nearby they were beating a nigger. They claimed he had somehow started the fire. Whatever the truth of that, his screams were dreadful. For several days afterwards I saw him sitting in a little patch of shade, looking terribly ill and trying to recover. Then he got up and went away. Without a sound, the wilderness took him back into its bosom. As I came from the darkness towards the glow, I found myself behind two men in conversation. I heard Kurtz’s name, followed by ‘take advantage of this unfortunate accident.’ One of them was the manager. I said good evening to him. ‘Have you ever seen anything like it, eh? Unbelievable,’ he replied, and left. The other stayed. He was a first-class agent, young, gentlemanly, rather reserved, with a little forked beard and a hooked nose. He kept the other agents at a distance. They, in return, called him the manager’s spy. Until then I had scarcely exchanged a word with him. We began talking, and after a while drifted away from the hissing remains of the shed. He invited me to his room in the station’s main building. When he lit a match, I discovered that this young aristocrat possessed not only a dressing-case with silver fittings but an entire candle for his exclusive use. At that time, candles were supposedly the manager’s privilege alone. Native mats hung on the clay walls, along with trophy displays of spears, assegais, shields, and knives. I had been told that this man’s assigned work was brickmaking. Yet not a piece of brick could be found in the station, although he had spent more than a year there, waiting. Apparently he needed some material before he could make bricks. I cannot say what; perhaps straw. Whatever it was, it could not be found locally and was unlikely to arrive from Europe, so I could not see what he expected to happen. Some special act of creation, perhaps. All sixteen or twenty of those pilgrims were waiting for something. From the way they went about it, I must say they appeared to enjoy the occupation. As far as I could tell, disease was the only thing that ever arrived for them. They passed their time with petty slander and foolish little schemes against one another. The station had an atmosphere of conspiracy. Naturally, none of it produced anything. It was as unreal as the rest: the entire concern’s charitable pretensions, its talk, its government, its appearance of work. The only genuine emotion was longing for an appointment to a post with ivory available, where commissions could be earned. That alone drove their plotting, slandering, and mutual hatred. But actually doing anything useful, even lifting a little finger—certainly not. By heavens! Perhaps the world has a point in letting one man steal a horse while refusing another even a glance at a halter. Steal a horse outright: very well, you have accomplished something, and perhaps you can ride it. But some ways of looking at a halter would make the kindest saint want to kick.

“What had made him seek my company I could not tell. As we talked, though, I suddenly realized that he was after something; in fact he was drawing me out for information. He kept bringing up Europe and the people he assumed I knew, asking suggestive questions about my connections in that sepulchral city and so forth. His small eyes shone with curiosity like little discs of mica, though he tried to maintain a faintly superior air. At first I was bewildered. Soon, however, I was intensely curious to discover what he could learn from me. I could not imagine possessing anything that would reward his efforts. Watching him defeat himself was delightful. In truth, I had nothing in my body except chills and nothing in my head except the miserable business of the steamboat. Clearly he thought me a shameless evader of the truth. Eventually he grew angry and covered a furious twitch of irritation with a yawn. I stood up. At that moment I noticed a little oil sketch painted on a panel: a draped woman, blindfolded, holding a burning torch. Behind her lay an almost black darkness. She moved with stately dignity, and the torch cast an ominous light on her face.

“The picture held my attention. He waited politely beside me, holding the candle in an empty half-pint champagne bottle—medical comforts. When I asked, he explained that Mr. Kurtz had painted it at this very station more than a year earlier, while waiting for transport to his trading-post. ‘Please tell me,’ I said, ‘who exactly is this Mr. Kurtz?’

“‘He runs the Inner Station,’ came the curt reply, with his eyes turned away. ‘Thank you very much,’ I said, laughing. ‘And you make bricks at the Central Station. Everybody knows as much as that.’ For a little time he said nothing. Then: ‘He is a prodigy. A messenger of pity, science, progress, and the devil knows what else. What we need,’ he suddenly began to proclaim, ‘to direct the cause Europe has, so to speak, placed in our hands, is superior intelligence, generous sympathies, a single purpose.’ ‘Who says so?’ I asked. ‘Plenty of people,’ he answered. ‘Some put it in writing. That is why _he_ comes out here, a special being, as you ought to know.’ Truly surprised, I interrupted: ‘Why should I know?’ He took no notice. ‘Yes. Today he commands the best station; next year he will be assistant-manager; another two years and... but you probably know what position he will hold in two years. You belong to the new gang, the virtuous gang. The people who sent him here specially are the same people who recommended you. Don’t deny it. I trust my own eyes.’ Then I understood. My dear aunt’s powerful friends had made an unforeseen impression on this young man. I almost laughed aloud. ‘Do you read the Company’s confidential letters?’ I asked. He was speechless. I enjoyed that enormously. ‘Once Mr. Kurtz becomes General Manager,’ I went on sternly, ‘you will have no such opportunity.’

“Without warning he blew out the candle, and we went into the open air. The moon was up. Black figures wandered wearily about, tipping water onto the glowing ruins. They hissed, and steam rose in the moonlight. Somewhere the beaten nigger was groaning. ‘What a din that brute is making!’ The tireless man with moustaches appeared beside us. ‘He deserves it. Offence, punishment, bang! No mercy, no mercy. There is no other way. We shall have no more conflagrations after this. I was just saying to the manager...’ He caught sight of my companion, and his spirits dropped instantly. ‘Still up,’ he said with a sort of servile good humour. ‘Quite natural. Ha! Danger, excitement.’ He disappeared. I walked on towards the river, with the other man following. Close to my ear came a contemptuous mutter: ‘Heap of muffs—go to.’ Groups of pilgrims stood arguing and waving their arms. Several still held their staffs. I really believe they slept with those sticks. Beyond the fence, the forest rose like a ghost in the moonlight. Through the faint movement and sounds of that wretched yard, the land’s silence reached into your heart: its mystery and immensity, the astonishing reality of the life it hid. Nearby the injured nigger gave a weak moan, then a deep sigh that made me quicken my steps away. A hand slipped under my arm. ‘My dear sir,’ the man began, ‘I would hate to be misunderstood, particularly by you. You will meet Mr. Kurtz long before I have that pleasure. I should be sorry if he formed a mistaken impression of my character....’

“I allowed this _papier-mache_ Mephistopheles to talk on. I felt that, if I chose, I could push a forefinger through him and discover nothing inside but perhaps a little loose dirt. You see, he had intended eventually to become assistant-manager under the present manager, and Kurtz’s arrival had plainly disturbed them both considerably. He spoke in a rush, and I made no effort to interrupt. My shoulders rested against the wrecked steamer, dragged up the slope like the carcass of some great river beast. Mud filled my nostrils—primeval mud, by Jove! Before my eyes stood the profound stillness of the primeval forest. Shining patches lay on the dark creek. Moonlight had silvered everything thinly: the rank grass, the mud, the tangled vegetation rising higher than a temple wall. Through a dark opening I saw the great river gleaming, gleaming, flowing broadly past without a sound. All of it was immense, waiting, speechless, while the man rattled on about himself. I wondered whether that still expression on the immensity facing the two of us was an appeal or a threat. Who were we, wandering into this place? Could we master this silent thing, or would it master us? I felt its size, its damned enormous size, this thing unable to speak and perhaps unable to hear. What did it contain? A little ivory came out of it before my eyes, and I had heard that Mr. Kurtz was somewhere within it. Heaven knows I had heard enough of that! Still, the information called up no picture, any more than news of an angel or a devil living there would have done. I accepted it as one of you might accept that Mars has inhabitants. I once knew a Scotch sailmaker who was certain, absolutely certain, that people lived on Mars. Ask him what they looked like or how they behaved, and he became shy and muttered something about ‘walking on all-fours.’ The smallest smile would make him challenge you to a fight, though he was sixty. I would not have fought for Kurtz, but on his behalf I came close enough to lying. You know how I hate lies, loathe them, cannot endure them. It is not that I am more honest than everyone else. They simply horrify me. Lies carry a stain of death, a taste of mortality: precisely what I hate in the world, what I want to put out of mind. They make me wretched and sick, as biting into something rotten would. A matter of temperament, I suppose. Well, I approached a lie by letting that young fool imagine anything he liked about my influence in Europe. In a moment I became as false as the other spellbound pilgrims. All because I somehow thought it might help Kurtz, whom I could not then picture, you understand. To me he was only a word. The name showed me no more of the man than it shows you. Can you see him? Can you see the story? Can you see anything at all? I feel I am attempting to describe a dream, attempting the impossible. No account of a dream can communicate the sensation of dreaming: that mixture of absurdity, astonishment, confusion, and the trembling effort to rebel; that feeling of captivity to the unbelievable which is what dreams essentially are....”
For a little time he said nothing.

“... No, it cannot be done. You cannot communicate the feeling of living through any particular stretch of your life—the thing that gives it truth and meaning, its delicate, all-pervading essence. It cannot be done. In life, as in dreams, each of us is alone....”
Again he fell quiet, apparently thinking; then he continued:
“Naturally, you can make out more in this than I could at the time. You can see me, someone you know....”

By now the darkness was so complete that those of us listening could barely make each other out. Marlow, sitting a little away from us, had long since become only a voice. None of us spoke. Perhaps the others had fallen asleep; I had not. I kept listening, waiting for some sentence, some word that might explain the faint disquiet the story produced in me. It seemed to be taking form by itself in the river’s thick night air, without any human mouth speaking it.

“... Yes, I let him talk,” Marlow resumed, “and imagine whatever he wanted about the powerful people supporting me. I did! And there was nothing behind me! Nothing except the miserable old steamboat, battered to pieces, against which I stood. All the while he spoke smoothly about ‘the necessity for every man to get on.’ ‘And when one comes out here, you conceive, it is not to gaze at the moon.’ Mr. Kurtz might be a ‘universal genius,’ but even genius worked more easily with ‘adequate tools—intelligent men.’ As for making bricks, he faced a physical impossibility, as I knew perfectly well. If he acted as the manager’s secretary, it was because ‘no sensible man rejects wantonly the confidence of his superiors.’ Did I understand? Certainly I understood. What else did I want? Rivets, by heaven, that was what I wanted! Rivets, so I could get on with the job and close the hole. All I wanted was rivets. Down on the coast stood crates of them, piled up, bursting apart, splitting open! In that station-yard on the hillside, every other step sent a loose rivet flying from under your foot. Some had rolled into the grove of death. Bend down and you could fill your pockets with them. Yet where rivets were actually needed, there was not a single one. We had suitable plates and nothing to attach them with. Every week our messenger, a tall negro with the letter-bag on his shoulder and a staff in his hand, set off for the coast. Several times each week, caravans arrived from there with goods for trade: dreadful shiny calico that made you shiver at the sight, glass beads worth perhaps a penny a quart, damned spotted cotton handkerchiefs. Never a rivet. Three carriers could have brought enough to float that steamboat again.

“He was now speaking in confidence. Eventually, though, my lack of response must have infuriated him, because he felt obliged to declare that he feared neither God nor devil, much less any ordinary man. I said that was perfectly clear to me. But what I needed was a supply of rivets, and rivets were what Mr. Kurtz needed too, if only he understood it. Now, letters travelled to the coast every week.... ‘My dear sir,’ he exclaimed, ‘I write from dictation.’ I insisted on the rivets. An intelligent man could find a way. His manner changed and turned icy. Abruptly he began discussing a hippopotamus. Since I slept aboard the steamer—I stayed with my salvage day and night—he wondered whether it disturbed me. An old hippo had the tiresome habit of climbing onto the bank at night and wandering through the station. The pilgrims would come out together and fire at it with every rifle they could find. Some had even stayed awake waiting for it. None of that effort achieved anything. ‘That animal has a charmed life,’ he observed. ‘But here one can say that only about beasts. No man—do you understand me?—no man in this country has a charmed life.’ He paused in the moonlight, his fine hooked nose a little to one side, his mica-like eyes shining without blinking. Then he gave me a curt good-night and marched away. I could tell he was unsettled and thoroughly confused. That gave me more hope than I had felt in days. What a relief to turn from him to my influential friend: the battered, warped, wrecked, tin-pot steamboat. I climbed aboard. Underfoot she rang like an empty Huntley & Palmer biscuit-tin being kicked down a gutter. She was less sturdily built, and rather less attractive in shape, but I had worked on her hard enough to grow fond of her. No powerful friend could have done more for me. She let me show something of myself and discover what I could do. No, I do not enjoy work. I would sooner idle about thinking of all the splendid things one might accomplish. I dislike work—every man does—but I like what it contains: the opportunity to discover yourself. Your own reality, known to you and not to others, something nobody else can ever know. They see only the outside performance and can never understand its actual meaning.

“Finding someone seated aft on the deck, his legs hanging above the mud, did not surprise me. I had become fairly friendly with the station’s few mechanics. Naturally the other pilgrims despised them, presumably because their manners lacked polish. This was their foreman, a boiler-maker by trade, and a capable worker. Thin and bony, with a yellow face and large, intent eyes, he looked anxious. His head was bare as my palm. But as the hair fell off, it seemed to have caught on his chin and thrived there: his beard reached his waist. A widower with six small children, he had left them with his sister when he came out. His great passion was pigeon-flying. He knew all about it and loved it extravagantly; he could go into raptures over pigeons. After work he sometimes walked over from his hut to talk about the children and the birds. When working, if he needed to crawl under the steamer through the mud, he bundled his beard into a sort of white napkin brought especially for the purpose, with loops that fitted over his ears. In the evening you could see him crouching at the water’s edge, carefully washing that wrapping in the creek, then solemnly laying it over a bush to dry.

“I thumped his back and cried, ‘We’re going to get rivets!’ He jumped up. ‘No! Rivets!’ he exclaimed, as if he could not trust his hearing. Then more quietly: ‘You... eh?’ Why we behaved like madmen I cannot say. I touched a finger to my nose and gave a mysterious nod. ‘Good for you!’ he shouted, raising one foot and clicking his fingers over his head. I attempted a jig. We pranced about on the iron deck. The wreck gave out a tremendous racket, which the untouched forest across the creek echoed in a thunderous roll over the sleeping station. Some of the pilgrims must have sat upright in their hovels. A dark shape blocked the manager’s lit doorway, disappeared, and a moment later the doorway’s light disappeared too. We stopped dancing. From deep within the land, the silence our feet had scattered flowed back. The immense wall of plants stood motionless in the moonlight, a luxuriant tangle of trunks, branches, leaves, boughs, and hanging garlands. It resembled an invasion of life surging forward without sound, a wave of vegetation heaped up and crested, about to break across the creek and sweep every little one of us out of his little life. Yet nothing moved. From far away came a muffled eruption of enormous splashes and snorting, as if an icthyosaurus were bathing in the great river’s glitter. ‘After all,’ the boiler-maker said sensibly, ‘what reason is there for the rivets not to come?’ What reason indeed! I could think of none. ‘We’ll have them in three weeks,’ I told him with confidence.

“They never came. What arrived in their place was an invasion, a plague, a visitation. During the following three weeks it appeared in successive sections. At the head of each was a donkey bearing a white man in fresh clothes and tan shoes, bowing from his elevated seat to the admiring pilgrims on either side. Close behind the donkey trudged a quarrelsome crowd of sullen niggers with sore feet. Tents, folding camp-stools, tin boxes, white cases, and brown bundles were dumped into the yard, and a little more mystery settled over the station’s confusion. Five of these batches arrived. Their ridiculous appearance suggested a disorderly retreat with loot from countless outfitters and food stores, as though, after a raid, they were hauling everything into the wilderness to divide it fairly. It was a hopeless tangle of perfectly respectable objects that human stupidity had made resemble stolen plunder.

“These dedicated men styled themselves the Eldorado Exploring Expedition. I believe they had taken an oath of secrecy. Their conversation, however, belonged to grubby buccaneers: reckless but without toughness, greedy but without boldness, cruel but without courage. Between them they had not a scrap of foresight or serious purpose. They seemed unaware that doing anything in the world requires such qualities. Their ambition was to rip treasure from the land’s entrails, with no higher moral aim than burglars forcing open a safe. Who funded this noble undertaking I cannot tell you. Our manager’s uncle, though, was the gang’s commander.

“He looked like a butcher from a poor district, with sleepy cunning in his eyes. His short legs carried a fat belly that he displayed proudly. Throughout his band’s infestation of the station, his nephew was the only person he addressed. All day you could watch the pair roaming about, heads close together, in a conversation that never ended.

“By then I had stopped tormenting myself over the rivets. There is less room in a person for that particular sort of foolishness than you might think. Hang! I said, and left things to drift. With ample time to reflect, I occasionally turned my thoughts towards Kurtz. I had no great interest in him. No. Still, I did wonder whether this man, who had arrived with some sort of moral ideas among his equipment, would really reach the top, and how he would go about his work once he got there.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: “One evening I lay stretched on the steamboat’s deck and heard voices coming closer. The manager and his uncle were walking along the bank. I rested my head on my arm again and was almost asleep when a voice seemed to speak straight into my ear: ‘I am as harmless as a little child, but I will not be ordered about. Am I the manager or not? They told me to send him there. Unbelievable.’ ... Then I realized that the two men had stopped beside the forward part of the boat, on the bank just beneath my head. I stayed still. Being sleepy, I never thought of moving. ‘It _is_ disagreeable,’ the uncle grunted. ‘He applied to the Administration for that posting,’ the manager went on, ‘so that he could demonstrate his abilities. And they instructed me accordingly. Think how much influence he must possess. Frightful, isn’t it?’ They agreed on its frightfulness, then exchanged some extraordinary fragments: ‘Make rain and fine weather—one man—the Council—by the nose.’ Those scraps of nonsense gradually overcame my sleepiness. I was almost fully alert when the uncle said, ‘Perhaps the climate will remove the difficulty for you. Is he there alone?’ ‘Yes,’ the manager replied. ‘He sent his assistant downriver with this note for me: “Clear this poor devil out of the country, and don’t bother sending more of that sort. I had rather be alone than have the kind of men you can dispose of with me.” That was over a year ago. Imagine the insolence!’ ‘Anything after that?’ the other asked hoarsely. ‘Ivory,’ the nephew snapped. ‘Plenty of it. The finest quality. Plenty.
