Coming from him, most irritating.’ ‘And accompanying it?’ came the deep rumble. ‘Invoice,’ shot back the answer. Silence followed. Their subject had been Kurtz.

“I was thoroughly awake now, but comfortable where I lay and without any reason to shift. ‘How did the ivory reach here from all that way?’ the older man growled, apparently much annoyed. The manager explained that a flotilla of canoes had brought it, commanded by an English half-caste clerk employed by Kurtz. Apparently Kurtz had meant to return too, since his station had run out of trade goods and supplies. But three hundred miles into the journey he had suddenly decided to turn back. He set off alone in a small dugout with four paddlers, leaving the half-caste to carry the ivory on downstream. Both men seemed astonished that anyone would attempt it; neither could find a sufficient reason. For my part, I felt I had caught my first glimpse of Kurtz. It was quite clear: the dugout, the four savage paddlers, the solitary white man abruptly turning away from headquarters, from relief, perhaps from thoughts of home, and facing back into the wilderness towards his empty, desolate station. His motive was unknown to me. Perhaps he was simply a decent man who loved his work for itself. His name, you understand, had never once been spoken. He was ‘that man.’ The half-caste, who seemed to have managed a difficult voyage with remarkable care and courage, was always ‘that scoundrel.’ The ‘scoundrel’ had reported that the ‘man’ had been very sick and had not fully recovered.... Below me the pair moved a few paces away and began strolling back and forth. Fragments reached me: ‘Military post—doctor—two hundred miles—quite alone now—unavoidable delays—nine months—no news—strange rumours.’ They came close again as the manager said, ‘Nobody that I know of, except a sort of itinerant trader, a pest of a fellow who grabs ivory from the natives.’ Who was this new subject? From scattered words I gathered that someone was believed to be operating in Kurtz’s district, someone the manager disliked. ‘We shall never be rid of unfair competition until one of them is hanged as a warning,’ he declared. ‘Certainly,’ grunted his companion. ‘Have him hanged! Why not? Anything is possible in this country, anything. As I say, nobody here—understand me, _here_—can threaten your position. Why? Because the climate agrees with you. You survive them all. Europe is where the danger lies, but before leaving I took care to—’ They walked off, whispering, then raised their voices again. ‘This exceptional succession of delays is not my responsibility. I did everything possible.’ The fat man sighed. ‘Very sad.’ The other continued: ‘And his talk is such poisonous nonsense. He plagued me with it when he was here. “Each station should be like a beacon on the road towards better things, a centre for trade of course, but also for humanizing, improving, instructing.” Just imagine that ass! And he hopes to become manager! No, it’s—’ Indignation choked him. I lifted my head slightly and was startled to find them directly underneath me. I could have spat onto their hats. Both stared thoughtfully at the ground. The manager flicked a slender twig against his leg. His wise relative looked up. ‘Have you kept well since coming out this time?’ he asked. The manager started. ‘Who? Me? Oh! Perfectly, perfectly. But everyone else—good heavens! All ill. And they die so fast I cannot get them out of the country in time. Incredible!’ ‘Hm’m. Exactly,’ the uncle grunted. ‘Ah! My boy, put your trust in this. This, I tell you.’ His short, flipper-like arm swept out to include the forest, creek, mud, and river. Before the land’s sunlit face, that dishonouring flourish seemed to summon its lurking death, its concealed evil, the darkness deep within its heart, in a treacherous appeal. It startled me so much that I jumped up and looked towards the forest’s edge, as though expecting a reply to that sinister declaration of faith. You know the foolish thoughts that sometimes seize you. The lofty stillness faced those two figures with threatening patience, waiting for their fantastic invasion to pass.

“They both swore out loud, from pure fright, I think. Then, pretending I did not exist, they headed back towards the station. The sun was sinking. Bent forward side by side, they seemed painfully to drag uphill their two absurd shadows, one longer than the other. Those shadows crept behind them over the tall grass without bending a blade.

“A few days later the Eldorado Expedition entered the waiting wilderness. It shut around them as water shuts over a diver. Much later we heard that every donkey had died. Of the less valuable animals’ fate I know nothing. Like the rest of us, they doubtless received their deserts. I made no enquiries. By then I was rather excited about seeing Kurtz soon. Soon is a relative word, of course. Exactly two months passed between our departure from the creek and our arrival at the bank beneath his station.

“Travelling upriver felt like returning to the world’s earliest days, when plants overran the earth and enormous trees ruled it. An unpeopled river, a vast silence, forest no one could penetrate. The air hung warm, dense, heavy, and sluggish. Even the brilliant sunlight gave no pleasure. Empty stretches of water extended into shadowed distances. Hippos and alligators lay together in the sun on silver sand-banks. Where the river broadened, it flowed among crowds of wooded islands. You could lose yourself there as completely as in a desert. All day you bumped against shallows, searching for the channel, until you felt bewitched and permanently severed from everything you had once known somewhere far away, perhaps in another life. Sometimes the past returned, as it will when you have no time at all for yourself. But it came as a restless, noisy dream, remembered with amazement amid the overwhelming facts of this alien world of vegetation, water, and silence. There was nothing peaceful about that living stillness. It belonged to a relentless power brooding over a purpose no one could read. It seemed to regard you with vengeance. Later I grew accustomed to it and ceased to notice; I had no time. I was forever guessing where the channel lay, recognizing submerged banks mostly by instinct, watching for rocks beneath the surface. I learned to snap my teeth shut before my heart escaped whenever sheer luck took us past some devilish hidden snag that could have torn the flimsy steamer apart and drowned every pilgrim. I had to spot dead timber we could cut at night to fuel the following day’s journey. Concentrate on such matters, these mere events upon the surface, and reality—the reality, I tell you—recedes. Mercifully, mercifully, the truth underneath stays concealed. Even so I felt it, often felt that mysterious stillness observing my monkey tricks, just as it observes you fellows performing on your separate tight-ropes for—what is it? Half-a-crown for each tumble—”
“Do try to be polite, Marlow,” someone growled. So at least one other listener besides me was still awake.

“My apologies. I left out the heartache that accounts for the remainder of the fee. And really, what does the fee matter if the trick is properly performed? You perform yours admirably. Nor did I do too badly, since I kept the steamer from sinking on my first voyage. That still astonishes me. Picture a blindfolded driver taking a van down a dreadful road. The business gave me plenty of sweating and shivering, I assure you. For a sailor, scraping the bottom of a vessel entrusted to him to keep afloat is, after all, the unforgivable sin. Nobody else need learn of it, but that impact never leaves you, does it? It strikes you in the heart. You remember it, dream about it, wake in the night thinking of it years later, and turn hot and cold. I cannot claim we always floated. Several times she had to wade a little, with twenty cannibals splashing about and pushing her. We had recruited some of these men along the way. Good fellows, those cannibals, in their proper place. You could work with them, and I remain grateful. After all, they did not eat one another in front of me. They carried a supply of hippo-meat instead, which rotted and gave the mysterious wilderness a stink in my nostrils. Phoo! I can smell it still. The manager was aboard, along with three or four pilgrims, each equipped with his staff. Occasionally we found a station on the bank, clinging to the edge of the unknown. White men would rush from a collapsing hut, gesturing with joy, surprise, and welcome. They looked strangely like captives held there by a spell. For a little while ‘ivory’ rang through the air. Then we moved back into silence, along deserted reaches and around motionless bends. The tall walls of our winding route threw back hollow echoes of the stern-wheel’s heavy pounding. Trees upon trees, millions of them, immense and solid and soaring. At their feet our little dirty steamboat crept close to the bank against the current, like a sluggish beetle crawling across the floor of a towering portico. You felt tiny and utterly lost, though the feeling was not wholly depressing. Small as you were, the grimy beetle kept advancing, which was all you asked. Where the pilgrims believed it was going I cannot say. Somewhere they expected to acquire something, I’ll wager! For me its only destination was Kurtz. But once the steam-pipes began leaking, our crawl grew very slow. The river opened ahead and closed behind, as though the forest had calmly stepped across the water to prevent our return. Deeper and deeper we travelled into the heart of darkness. The quiet there was profound. Sometimes at night drums sounded beyond the screen of trees. Their rumble travelled upriver and lingered faintly, seeming to hang high above us until dawn’s first light. War, peace, prayer: we could not tell what it meant. Before dawn a cold stillness descended. The wood-cutters slept beside low-burning fires, and a snapping twig made you jump. We wandered across a prehistoric earth, an earth that looked like an unfamiliar planet. We might have imagined ourselves the first men claiming an accursed inheritance, one to be subdued only through terrible suffering and immense labour. Then, struggling around a bend, we would suddenly glimpse rush walls and pointed grass roofs: a burst of shouting, whirling black limbs, clapping hands, stamping feet, swaying bodies, rolling eyes beneath the heavy drooping leaves that never stirred. Slowly the steamer laboured beside a dark frenzy we could not comprehend. Was prehistoric man cursing us, praying to us, welcoming us? Who could know? Understanding our surroundings was beyond us. We passed like ghosts, bewildered and secretly horrified, as sane men might witness a spirited outbreak in a madhouse. We were too far removed to understand, and could not remember. Our journey lay through the night of the earliest ages, ages long vanished, leaving scarcely a trace and no memories.

“The earth itself seemed otherworldly. We are used to seeing a conquered monster in chains. Here you could see something monstrous that remained free. Unearthly, yes, and the men were—No, not inhuman. That, you understand, was the worst part: the suspicion that they were human. The realization dawned slowly. They screamed, jumped, whirled, and twisted their faces horribly. Yet what sent a thrill through you was their humanity, so like your own, your distant kinship with that wild, passionate tumult. Ugly, certainly. But a man with enough courage would acknowledge some faint answering impulse within himself, some dim recognition of meaning in that noise’s terrible openness. Even you, so far removed from the night of the earliest ages, could understand it. Why should you not? The human mind can contain anything, because everything is already within it: the whole past and the whole future. What was actually there? Happiness, fear, grief, devotion, bravery, anger—who could say? But truth, truth with its covering of time stripped off. A fool can gape and tremble; a man understands and watches without flinching. He must, though, be at least as much a man as those people on the bank. To meet their truth he needs his own genuine substance, his native strength. Principles are useless. They are acquired things, clothes, pretty rags blown away by the first real shaking. What you need is a belief deliberately held. Does that devilish uproar appeal to something in me? Very well: I hear it, I acknowledge it. But I too possess a voice, and whether for good or evil, my speech will not be silenced. A fool, naturally, stays safe behind sheer terror and noble sentiments. Who is grunting there? You wonder why I did not land and join the howling and dancing? No, I did not. Noble sentiments? To hell with noble sentiments! I had no time. I was busy with white-lead and woollen blanket strips, helping bandage those leaking steam-pipes, I tell you. I had to watch our course, dodge snags, and somehow keep that tin-pot moving. The surface-truth in those duties would have saved a wiser man than me. Between times I supervised our savage fireman. He was an improved specimen, able to stoke a vertical boiler. Looking down at him, I assure you, was as instructive as watching a dog walk upright in imitation trousers and a feathered hat. A few months’ instruction had brought that truly fine fellow to this. He peered at the steam and water gauges, visibly summoning bravery. The poor devil had filed teeth, odd patterns shaved into his woolly hair, and three decorative scars on each cheek. He should have been on the bank clapping and stamping. Instead he worked hard, enslaved to unfamiliar magic and loaded with improving knowledge. Training made him useful. This was what he understood: if the water vanished from the clear tube, the evil spirit in the boiler would grow furiously thirsty and exact a dreadful revenge. So he sweated, fed the fire, and watched the glass in fear. A makeshift rag charm was tied to his arm; a flat, polished piece of bone as large as a watch pierced his lower lip. Meanwhile the forested banks slipped slowly past, the brief uproar fell behind, and through endless silent miles we crept towards Kurtz. But submerged snags crowded the shallow, deceptive water, the boiler really seemed to harbour a sulky devil, and neither of us had leisure to examine our disturbing thoughts.

“About fifty miles short of the Inner Station we found a reed hut, a dismal leaning pole flying the unrecognizable shreds of some former flag, and a carefully piled stack of wood. An unexpected sight. We drew alongside the bank and discovered a flat board on the firewood bearing faint pencil marks. Once deciphered, they read: ‘Wood for you. Hurry up. Approach cautiously.’ The signature could not be read, but it was much longer than Kurtz. ‘Hurry up.’ To where? Farther upriver? ‘Approach cautiously.’ We had certainly failed to do that. Yet surely the warning did not concern a place where it could only be discovered after one arrived. Something upstream was wrong. What, and how seriously? That was the puzzle. We criticized the idiocy of this telegram-like wording. The surrounding bush offered no answer and blocked our sight as well. A ripped red twill curtain hung across the hut’s entrance, flapping forlornly against our faces. The place had been stripped, though clearly a white man had lived there recently. A crude table remained, a board balanced on two posts. Rubbish lay in a dark corner. Beside the door I picked up a book. Its covers were gone and handling had worn its pages soft and filthy, but someone had carefully restitched its spine with white cotton that was still clean. What an extraordinary discovery. The title was _An Inquiry into some Points of Seamanship_, written by a Master in his Majesty’s Navy called Towser or Towson, something like that. The contents looked dull: explanatory diagrams and forbidding tables of numbers. This copy was sixty years old. I treated that astonishing relic with extreme gentleness, afraid it might crumble in my hands. Towson or Towser was seriously investigating the strain that would break ships’ chains and tackle, and similar questions. Hardly thrilling reading. Yet immediately you recognized a single-minded purpose, an honest interest in doing a job properly. Those modest pages, conceived so long ago, shone with a light beyond mere professional knowledge. Talking of chains and purchases, that straightforward old sailor made me forget the jungle and the pilgrims. I enjoyed the delicious feeling of finding something undeniably real. The presence of such a book was remarkable enough. More astonishing still were pencilled notes in the margins, plainly commenting on the text. I could scarcely trust my eyes! They were written in cipher! At least, that was how they looked. Imagine someone carrying this book into the middle of nowhere, studying it, and annotating it—in cipher! The mystery was extravagant.

“For some time a troublesome noise had barely entered my awareness. Looking up, I discovered that the wood-pile had vanished and the manager and all his pilgrims were shouting at me from the water’s edge. I pocketed the book. Believe me, stopping my reading felt like wrenching myself away from the protection of an old, dependable friendship.

“I set our crippled engine moving again. ‘It must belong to that wretched trader, that trespasser,’ the manager exclaimed, glaring back at the place. ‘An Englishman, surely,’ I remarked. ‘That will not keep him out of trouble unless he takes care,’ the manager muttered ominously. With pretended innocence, I observed that nobody in this world was beyond trouble’s reach.

“Now the current quickened. The steamer appeared to be drawing her final breath, her stern-wheel slapping weakly. I found myself almost rising onto my toes to listen for the next beat, so sure was I that the miserable vessel might stop at any instant. It was like watching a life’s last flickers. Nevertheless we crawled on. Occasionally I selected a tree ahead to measure our advance towards Kurtz, but always lost track of it before we came alongside. Human patience cannot hold its gaze on a single object that long. The manager exhibited an admirable resignation. I fretted, raged, and debated inwardly whether I should speak frankly to Kurtz. Before reaching any decision, I realized that speaking, keeping silent, or indeed doing anything would accomplish nothing. What difference did anyone’s knowledge or ignorance make? What difference who managed the business? Sometimes such understanding flashes over you. What mattered here lay far below the surface, out of my reach and beyond any interference I could make.

“Near dusk on the second day, we reckoned ourselves eight miles from Kurtz’s station. I wished to continue, but the manager grew solemn. Navigation there was dangerous, he said, and with the sun already so low, we ought to remain until morning. Besides, obedience to the instruction to approach cautiously required daylight, rather than twilight or darkness. His argument made sense. Eight miles would take us nearly three hours, and I could see troubling ripples at the far end of the reach. Still, the delay exasperated me beyond words. That was unreasonable: after months of waiting, another night could scarcely matter. With plenty of fuel and caution our watchword, I anchored midstream. The channel was straight and narrow, its high sides like a railway cutting. Twilight slid into it well before sunset. The water ran smoothly and fast; along the banks lay a speechless immobility. The trees bound together by creepers, and every living shrub beneath them, might have become stone, down to the finest twig and lightest leaf. It was no sleep. It seemed unnatural, a trance. There was not the smallest sound. Watching in astonishment, you began to wonder whether you had lost your hearing. Then night fell abruptly and took your sight as well. Around three in the morning a big fish jumped. Its splash startled me like a gunshot. Sunrise brought a white fog, hot and clammy, more blinding than darkness. It neither drifted nor moved, merely stood around us like a solid substance. Perhaps at eight or nine it rose like a shutter. For an instant we saw the enormous tangled jungle and its countless towering trees, with the sun’s small blazing ball suspended above, all utterly still. Then the white shutter slid smoothly down again, as though its runners were greased. We had begun hauling in the anchor chain; I ordered it let out once more. Before its muffled clatter stopped, a cry rose slowly through the opaque air, a tremendous cry of seemingly boundless desolation. It ended. A lamenting uproar, changing through savage discords, filled our ears. Its complete unexpectedness made my hair stir beneath my cap. How the others felt I cannot say. To me the fog itself seemed to have screamed: the mournful tumult burst out so abruptly, apparently from every direction. It reached a rapid eruption of almost unbearably intense shrieking, then broke off. We stood frozen in assorted foolish poses, stubbornly listening to a silence nearly as overwhelming and frightening. ‘Good God! What can this mean—’ stammered a pilgrim beside me, a short, fat fellow with sandy hair, red whiskers, elastic-sided boots, and pink pyjamas tucked into his socks. Two others gaped for a full minute, dashed into the small cabin, and immediately reappeared clutching Winchesters at the ‘ready,’ their eyes darting fearfully. Nothing was visible except our steamer, its edges blurred as if dissolving, and perhaps two feet of mist-covered water around it. To our eyes and ears the rest of existence had ceased. It was nowhere. Simply nowhere. Vanished, swept away without leaving the faintest whisper or shadow.

“I went forward and told the men to shorten the anchor chain, so we could free the anchor and move immediately if necessary. ‘Are they going to attack?’ someone whispered in awe. ‘They will slaughter us all in this fog,’ another murmured. Strain twitched their faces, their hands shook a little, and their eyes ceased blinking. The difference between the white men’s expressions and those of our black crew fascinated me. The crew knew this stretch of river no better than we did, though their homes lay only eight hundred miles away. Besides their obvious agitation, the whites looked painfully affronted by such outrageous noise. The others appeared alert and naturally curious but fundamentally calm, including the one or two who grinned while hauling the chain. Several exchanged brief grunts that apparently settled the question to their satisfaction. Their headman stood near me, a young black man with a broad chest, fierce nostrils, and hair carefully arranged in oily curls. Dark-blue fringed cloths draped him severely. ‘Aha!’ I said, merely to be friendly. His bloodshot eyes widened, sharp teeth flashed. ‘Catch ’im,’ he snapped. ‘Catch ’im. Give ’im to us.’ ‘To you? And what would you do with them?’ I asked. ‘Eat ’im!’ he answered shortly. Resting an elbow on the rail, he stared into the fog with great dignity and deep thoughtfulness. I would undoubtedly have felt suitably horrified if it had not occurred to me how hungry he and his men must be. Their hunger must have been growing for at least a month. Their engagement was for six months. I doubt any of them clearly understood time as we do after countless ages; they still inhabited its beginnings, without inherited experience to instruct them, so to speak. Naturally, provided someone filled in a paper according to some ridiculous law invented downstream, nobody considered how they were to stay alive. They had brought rotten hippo-meat, certainly, but even without the pilgrims throwing much of it overboard amid a tremendous uproar, it could not have lasted long. That disposal looked arbitrary, but was really lawful self-defence. You cannot inhale dead hippo while awake, asleep, and eating and still maintain your precarious hold on life. Their other provision was a weekly payment of three brass wires, each about nine inches long. In theory this currency would buy food in riverside villages. You can imagine how _that_ succeeded. Either no village existed, or its people were hostile, or the director declined to stop for some obscure reason. He ate from tins like the rest of us, with the occasional elderly he-goat added. Unless the crew swallowed the wire or bent it into loops to catch fish, I cannot see how their lavish wages helped them. I must acknowledge the payments arrived with a punctuality befitting a great and honourable trading company. Apart from that, their only food I saw was a few lumps resembling partly cooked dough, a dirty lavender colour. It looked thoroughly inedible. Wrapped in leaves, it yielded occasional mouthfuls so tiny that eating them seemed a ceremony rather than a serious attempt at nourishment. Looking back, I am astonished that, with thirty of them against five of us, all the gnawing devils of hunger never drove them to attack us and enjoy one substantial meal. They were large, powerful men, little inclined to calculate consequences, brave and still strong, though their skin had lost its sheen and their muscles their firmness. Some restraint was operating, one of those secrets of human conduct that defy probability. I watched them with suddenly awakened interest. Not because I expected to be eaten shortly, although I admit I then saw the pilgrims’ unhealthy appearance in a new light and hoped, yes, positively hoped, that I did not look so—how shall I say?—so unappetizing. Such fantastic vanity suited the dreamlike quality of all my days then. Perhaps I also had a slight fever. One cannot perpetually keep a finger on one’s pulse. I often had ‘a little fever,’ or a touch of something else: the wilderness’s playful pawing before the serious attack that duly followed. Yes, I studied these men as one studies any human beings, wondering about their impulses, motives, abilities, and frailties when tested by an unyielding bodily need. Restraint! What could restrain them? Superstition, revulsion, patience, fear, some primitive honour? Hunger defeats fear, outlasts patience, abolishes disgust. Superstitions, beliefs, principles, whatever you call them, scatter before it more easily than chaff in a breeze. Have you never known the devilishness of protracted starvation, its maddening pain, black thoughts, brooding savagery? I have. Resisting hunger properly demands every ounce of a man’s natural strength. Bereavement, disgrace, even the loss of one’s soul are easier to confront than prolonged hunger of that sort. A sorrowful truth. And these men had no conceivable reason for scruples. Restraint! I would as readily have expected it from a hyena roaming a battlefield’s dead. Yet the fact confronted me, dazzling and visible, like foam on the sea’s depths, a ripple over an unmeasurable enigma. Thinking about it, I found this mystery greater than the strange, inexplicable despair in the savage cries that had passed us on the riverbank behind the fog’s blinding whiteness.

“Two pilgrims argued in rapid whispers about which shore. ‘Left.’ ‘No, no, how can you say that? Right, obviously right.’ Behind me the manager said, ‘A very serious situation. I should be devastated if anything happened to Mr. Kurtz before our arrival.’ I looked round, entirely convinced of his sincerity. He was precisely the sort who wanted appearances maintained. That was what restrained him. But when he muttered that we should continue immediately, I did not bother replying. He knew as well as I that we could not. Once detached from the bottom, we would be suspended in empty space. We could not know whether we travelled upstream, downstream, or sideways until we hit a bank, and even then would initially be unable to identify which bank it was. Naturally I stayed put. I had no desire to wreck the vessel. A more fatal place for a shipwreck was unimaginable. If we escaped immediate drowning, some other quick death was certain. After a pause he said, ‘I give you authority to accept every risk.’ ‘I will accept none,’ I replied sharply. He had expected the answer, though perhaps not my tone. ‘Then I must accept your judgment. You are the captain,’ he said with elaborate courtesy. To show my gratitude, I turned a shoulder towards him and stared into the fog. How long could it continue? Nothing looked more hopeless. Reaching this Kurtz, who grubbed for ivory in that wretched bush, involved as many perils as reaching an enchanted princess asleep in a legendary castle. In a confidential voice the manager asked, ‘Do you believe they will attack?’

“Several clear reasons made an attack seem unlikely. First, the dense fog: any canoes leaving shore would become as lost as we would if we moved. Admittedly I had also considered the jungle on both banks impenetrable, yet eyes within it had observed us. The riverside bushes were certainly thick, but people could evidently pass through the growth behind. Still, during the fog’s brief lifting I had seen no canoes anywhere, certainly none alongside us. What made an attack unthinkable to me, though, was the character of those cries. They lacked the ferocity that announces immediate violence. Sudden, wild, and loud as they were, they had conveyed an overwhelming sorrow. For some reason, seeing the steamboat had filled those savages with uncontrollable grief. I explained that any danger arose from our nearness to a great human passion released without restraint. Extreme grief can eventually discharge itself in violence, but usually settles into apathy....

“You should have seen their faces! They could neither smile nor curse me. I think they believed fear had driven me mad. I gave them quite a lecture. My dear fellows, worrying accomplished nothing. Keep watch? You may be sure I watched for the fog to lift as intently as a cat watches a mouse. For any other purpose our sight was as useless as though miles of cotton-wool lay piled over us. It felt that way too: warm, suffocating, choking. Moreover, extravagant as my explanation sounded, it fitted the facts exactly. What we later called an attack was actually an effort to repel us. It was far from an aggressive act, nor even defensive in the ordinary meaning. Desperation prompted it, and its essential object was protection.

“The incident began, I should say, about two hours after the mist cleared, at a place roughly a mile and a half downstream from Kurtz’s station. We had just struggled and flapped around a bend when a tiny island appeared in midstream, little more than a bright-green mound of grass. Nothing else of that kind was visible. As more of the reach opened before us, however, I saw that it headed a long sand-bank, or rather a succession of shallow patches extending down the river’s centre. Discoloured and barely submerged, the entire chain showed through the water like a man’s backbone running beneath the skin down the middle of his back. So far as I could judge, a passage lay on either side. Naturally I knew neither channel. The banks looked much alike and the depth appeared equal. Since I had been told the station stood on the western side, I naturally steered into the western passage.

“Once inside the channel I realized it was far narrower than expected. On our left ran the unbroken shoal; on our right rose a steep, high bank thick with shrubs. Above them, trees stood in close ranks. Branches hung densely over the current, and here and there a heavy limb thrust stiffly across the water. Afternoon was well advanced. The forest’s face looked dark, and a broad shadow already covered the river beside it. We steamed through that shadow, very slowly, as you can imagine. I took her close inshore, since the sounding-pole showed the deepest water beside the bank.

“One of my hungry, patient friends worked the sounding-pole in the bows directly below me. Imagine a flat-bottomed, decked scow: that was our steamboat. Two small teak houses, fitted with doors and windows, stood on the deck. Forward was the boiler; the machinery sat right aft. A light canopy on upright supports covered everything. The funnel passed through it. Ahead of the funnel, a little cabin of thin planks formed the pilot-house, containing a couch, two camp-stools, a small table, the wheel, and a loaded Martini-Henry propped in a corner. A wide doorway faced forward, with a broad shutter on either side. Naturally all remained open. I spent my days perched outside the door at the roof’s foremost edge. At night I slept, or attempted to sleep, on the couch. Our helmsman was a muscular black man from a coastal tribe, trained by my unfortunate predecessor. He wore brass earrings and a blue cloth from waist to ankles and considered himself extremely important. I had never met a more unreliable fool. With you beside him he steered with endless swagger. The moment he lost sight of you, utter terror seized him, and within minutes he let that crippled steamer overpower him.

“I was watching the sounding-pole with considerable irritation, because each sounding left a little more of it above water. Suddenly the man abandoned the task and dropped flat onto the deck. He did not even pull the pole aboard, though he kept his grip as it trailed in the river. Simultaneously the fireman, also visible beneath me, abruptly sat in front of his furnace and lowered his head. I was astonished. But a snag in our course forced my attention back to the water. Little sticks were flying everywhere, thickly: past my nose, down below, into the pilot-house behind me. Meanwhile river, shore, and forest remained entirely silent. Only the stern-wheel’s heavy splashing and the tapping of those objects reached my ears. We lurched past the obstruction. Arrows, by Jove! Someone was shooting at us! I hurried inside to close the landward shutter. The idiot at the wheel gripped its spokes while raising his knees, stamping, and working his mouth like a horse held on a tight rein. Damn him! We were wallowing scarcely ten feet from shore. To swing the heavy shutter I had to lean far outside. Among the leaves, level with my own, a face stared at me steadily and fiercely. Then a veil seemed to fall from my eyes. Deep within the tangled darkness I distinguished naked chests, arms, legs, shining eyes: the bush teemed with moving human limbs, gleaming bronze. Twigs shook and rustled, arrows shot out, and the shutter closed. ‘Keep her straight,’ I told the helmsman. His head stayed stiffly forward, but his eyes rolled. He continued gently lifting and lowering his feet, with a little foam at his mouth. ‘Stand still!’ I shouted furiously. I might as well have commanded a tree to resist the wind. I rushed outside. Beneath me feet scrambled on the metal deck, voices cried out confusedly, and someone screamed, ‘Can we turn round?’ Ahead appeared a V-shaped ripple. What now? Another snag! Gunfire erupted below my feet. The pilgrims were discharging their Winchesters, simply spraying bullets into the vegetation. A tremendous cloud of smoke rose and drifted ahead. I cursed it. Now both ripple and snag were invisible. I peered from the doorway as arrows came in clouds. They might carry poison, but looked too slight to kill a cat. Howling broke from the bush. Our wood-cutters answered with a war cry. A rifle fired immediately behind me and deafened me. I glanced back, then lunged for the wheel through the noise and smoke filling the pilot-house. The fool-nigger had abandoned everything, opened the shutter, and fired the Martini-Henry. He stood glaring through the opening. I shouted for him to come back while correcting the boat’s sudden swerve. Even if I wished to turn, there was no space. The snag lay somewhere close ahead in that damned smoke; we had no time. I drove her towards the bank, hard against it, where I knew deep water lay.

“Slowly we scraped through the overhanging vegetation, snapping twigs and scattering leaves. As expected, the shooting below ceased when their squirt-guns emptied. Something flashing whistled through the pilot-house, entering one shutter opening and leaving the other, and I jerked my head back. Beyond the crazed helmsman shaking his unloaded rifle and shouting ashore, I saw indistinct men running bent double, jumping, slipping past, briefly clear, half visible, gone. A large object appeared outside the shutter. The rifle flew overboard. The man stepped sharply backwards, gave me an extraordinary look over his shoulder—deep, intimate, familiar—and collapsed at my feet. His head struck the wheel twice. What looked like a long cane swung rattling about and upset a camp-stool. He seemed to have lost his balance pulling the thing away from someone ashore. The thin smoke had cleared and we had passed the snag. Ahead, perhaps a hundred yards farther, there would be room to pull away from shore. But my feet felt so warm and wet that I looked down. He lay on his back, gazing directly at me, both hands gripping the cane. It was a spear shaft. Thrown or thrust through the opening, its point had entered his side below the ribs, making a terrible wound and disappearing inside. My shoes were full. Beneath the wheel a still pool of blood gleamed dark red, and his eyes shone extraordinarily. The shooting began again. Anxiously he watched me, clutching the spear like a treasure, apparently afraid I would remove it. I struggled to break that gaze and concentrate on steering. Reaching overhead with one hand, I found the whistle cord and pulled out one piercing shriek after another. The angry war cries stopped instantly. From deep in the trees rose a long, trembling lament of terrified sorrow and absolute despair, such as might greet the departure of the earth’s last hope. The bush stirred violently; arrows stopped falling. A few isolated shots cracked, then silence returned, with the stern-wheel’s weak beat clearly audible. I put the helm hard to starboard just as the pink-pyjama pilgrim appeared in the doorway, flushed and excited. ‘The manager has sent me—’ he began formally, then stopped. ‘Good God!’ he said, staring at the wounded man.

“We two white men stood above him, both enclosed in his bright, questioning gaze. I swear he seemed about to ask us something in words we could understand. Instead he died without a sound, a movement, a single muscular twitch. Only at the final instant, responding perhaps to a sign invisible to us or an unheard whisper, he frowned deeply. That frown made his black death-mask look unimaginably dark, brooding, threatening. The questioning light quickly left his eyes, which became blank glass. ‘Can you handle the wheel?’ I asked the agent urgently. He looked doubtful, but I seized his arm and he understood that he would steer, capable or not. Frankly, changing my shoes and socks had become an almost morbid need. ‘He is dead,’ the man whispered, deeply affected. ‘Certainly,’ I replied, hauling frantically at my laces. ‘And I suppose Mr. Kurtz must be dead by now as well.’

“That thought possessed me for the moment. I felt profoundly disappointed, as if everything I had been struggling towards had proved entirely without substance. Had I travelled all that distance merely to speak with Mr. Kurtz, I could not have felt more disgusted. To speak with... I threw a shoe overboard and realized that was precisely what I had anticipated: a conversation with Kurtz. Strangely, I discovered I had never pictured him acting, only talking. My thought was neither ‘Now I will never see him’ nor ‘Now I will never shake him by the hand,’ but ‘Now I will never hear him.’ He appeared to me as a voice. Of course I associated him with actions too. Had I not heard, in every shade of envy and admiration, that he had gathered, traded for, cheated people out of, or stolen more ivory than all the other agents combined? But that was beside the point. He was a gifted being, and among his gifts one stood supreme, conveying an actual presence: speech, words, expression. Bewildering, revealing, exalted, contemptible; a throbbing current of light or a fraudulent stream flowing out of darkness no one could penetrate.

“I sent the second shoe flying to the river’s devil-god. ‘By Jove!’ I thought. ‘That finishes it. We have arrived too late. He is gone, his gift is gone, destroyed by an arrow, spear, or club. After all, I shall never hear the fellow speak.’ My grief carried a startling excess of feeling, like the howling grief of those savages in the forest. Losing a faith or missing my life’s appointed destiny could scarcely have left me more desolate or alone.... Who is sighing in that disgusting fashion? Absurd? Very well, absurd. Good Lord! Is a man never allowed—Here, pass the tobacco.”...

A deep stillness followed. Then a match flamed, revealing Marlow’s thin face, worn and hollow, its downward lines and lowered lids expressing intense concentration. As he drew hard on his pipe, the little flame’s steady flickering seemed to bring his face forward from the darkness and draw it back again. The match died.

“Absurd!” he exclaimed. “That is the trouble with trying to explain.... Here you sit, each secured by two respectable addresses like a hulk riding on two anchors, a butcher at one corner and a policeman at the next, healthy appetites, normal temperatures—normal, do you hear?—all year round. And your verdict is Absurd! Absurd be—blasted! Absurd! My dear fellows, what do you expect of someone who has just thrown perfectly new shoes overboard out of sheer nervous strain! Thinking back, I am amazed I did not weep. On the whole I admire my own courage. The thought of losing the priceless chance to hear the gifted Kurtz wounded me deeply. Naturally I was mistaken. That privilege still awaited me. Oh yes, I heard quite enough, and more. Yet I was right as well. A voice. Little beyond a voice. I heard him—it—that voice—and other voices. Nearly everything was merely voices. Even the memory of the period hangs invisibly about me, like the last trembling echo of an enormous, meaningless babble: foolish, dreadful, sordid, savage, or simply petty. Voices upon voices, even the girl herself, now—”
For a long while he said nothing.

“Eventually I laid the ghost of his gifts to rest by lying,” he said abruptly. “Girl! What? Did I speak of a girl? Oh, she has no part in it, none whatever. They—the women—are outside it, ought to remain outside it. We must keep them in that lovely world of theirs, or ours will grow worse. She had to be excluded. You should have heard that dug-up body of Mr. Kurtz pronounce ‘My Intended.’ Immediately you would have understood how completely she was excluded. And that high forehead of his! Hair supposedly continues growing sometimes, but this—ah—specimen was astonishingly bald. The wilderness had stroked his head, and behold, it resembled a ball, an ivory ball. Its caress had made him wither—lo! It had seized him, loved him, clasped him, entered his blood, eaten his flesh, and bound his soul to its own through the unimaginable rituals of some satanic initiation. He was its indulged, pampered favourite. Ivory? Indeed. Heaps and heaps of it. His old mud hut overflowed. You might have supposed no tusk remained anywhere in the country, above ground or below. ‘Mostly fossil,’ the manager had sneered. It was no more fossilized than I am. They use that name when ivory is dug up. Apparently these niggers sometimes bury tusks, but this lot had plainly not been buried deeply enough to keep the gifted Mr. Kurtz from his destiny. We packed the steamer with it and stacked a great quantity on deck too. There he could see and enjoy it for as long as sight remained, since gratitude for that favour lasted to the end. You should have heard ‘My ivory’ from his lips. Yes, I heard it. ‘My Intended, my ivory, my station, my river, my—’ He owned everything. I held my breath, expecting the wilderness to erupt in laughter so immense that it would shake the fixed stars from their places. Everything was his, but that hardly mattered. What mattered was whose he was, how many dark powers claimed possession of him. That reflection made your whole skin creep. Trying to imagine it was impossible, and unhealthy besides. He had literally taken an exalted seat among the land’s devils. You cannot understand. How could you, standing on firm pavements among helpful neighbours ready either to encourage you or attack you? You tread carefully between butcher and policeman, terrified of scandal, the gallows, the madhouse. How could you imagine which region of the earliest ages a man’s unfettered feet might reach through solitude, complete solitude without a policeman, and silence, absolute silence without a kindly neighbour whispering warnings about public opinion? Those small circumstances make the entire difference. Without them, your only resource is your native strength, your capacity to remain faithful. Perhaps you are too foolish to go astray, too dull even to recognize an assault by the powers of darkness. I suspect no fool ever sold his soul to the devil. Either the fool is too much a fool or the devil too much a devil; I cannot decide. Alternatively you may be so thunderously exalted that only heavenly sights and sounds reach you. For such a person the earth is merely somewhere to stand. Whether that state brings gain or loss I shall not claim to judge. Most of us, however, belong to neither sort. We inhabit the earth and must endure its sights and sounds and smells too, by Jove! We must, so to speak, breathe dead hippo without catching its corruption. That is where strength enters, you see: confidence in your ability to dig inconspicuous holes and bury the stuff, devotion to some obscure, exhausting task rather than to yourself. That is hard enough. Understand, I seek neither to excuse nor even explain; I am trying to account to myself for—for—Mr. Kurtz, the shadow of Mr. Kurtz. Before disappearing altogether, that initiated ghost from the back of Nowhere honoured me with remarkable confidences. He could speak English to me, that was why. The original Kurtz had received part of his education in England and, as he kindly informed me, held the proper sympathies. His mother was half-English and his father half-French. All Europe helped create him. Later I discovered that, very appropriately, the International Society for the Suppression of Savage Customs had commissioned a report from him to guide its future work. He wrote it. I have seen and read it. Eloquent, quivering with eloquence, though rather overwrought, I thought. He had found time for seventeen closely written pages! This must have preceded the disturbance of his—let us call them—nerves, which led him to preside at midnight dances concluding in unspeakable rites. From what I reluctantly pieced together at different times, those rites were dedicated to him—to Mr. Kurtz himself, do you understand? Still, the writing was beautiful. In light of later knowledge, its first paragraph now seems ominous. It argued that white men, given our stage of development, ‘must necessarily appear to them [savages] in the nature of supernatural beings—we approach them with the might of a deity,’ and so forth. ‘By the simple exercise of our will we can exert a power for good practically unbounded,’ etc., etc. From there he rose into the heights, carrying me along. His magnificent conclusion is hard to recall exactly. It suggested an exotic Immensity governed by a majestic Benevolence and made me thrill with enthusiasm. Such was the limitless force of eloquence, of words, of burning noble language. No practical advice disturbed that enchanted current, unless one counts a note scrawled at the foot of the last page, evidently much later, in a shaky hand, as a proposed method. The method was simple. After that moving appeal to every generous feeling, it flashed out, terrifyingly bright, like lightning across a peaceful sky: ‘Exterminate all the brutes!’ Curiously, he appeared to have forgotten that useful postscriptum. Later, when in a sense he returned to himself, he repeatedly begged me to guard ‘my pamphlet,’ as he called it, certain that it would benefit his future career. All these matters were fully disclosed to me. As things turned out, his memory too was placed in my care. I have done enough for it to earn the unquestionable right, if I wish, to consign it for ever to progress’s dust-bin, among civilization’s sweepings and, metaphorically, its dead cats. But I cannot choose to do so. He refuses to be forgotten. Whatever else he was, he was no ordinary man. He could charm or terrify rudimentary souls into an intensified witch-dance celebrating him, and could fill the pilgrims’ little souls with bitter apprehension. He possessed at least one faithful friend, and had won one soul neither rudimentary nor stained by selfish ambition. No, I cannot forget him. Yet I will not assert that he was worth the life spent reaching him. I missed my dead helmsman terribly, even while his body still lay in the pilot-house. Perhaps such sorrow for a savage, no more significant than one sand-grain in a black Sahara, seems extraordinary to you. But he had accomplished something: he steered. For months he stood behind me as helper, as instrument. A partnership of sorts. He steered for me; I cared for him and worried about his shortcomings. That made a delicate bond whose existence I recognized only when it snapped. His deeply intimate look when he was wounded remains with me still, like a distant kinship claiming recognition at the supreme instant.

“Poor idiot! If only he had not touched the shutter. No restraint, none at all, just like Kurtz, a tree bending to the wind. Once I had put on dry slippers, I dragged him outside. First I pulled the spear from his side, keeping my eyes tightly shut, I admit. His heels bounced together across the little threshold. His shoulders pressed against my chest as I desperately clasped him from behind. Oh! How heavy he was, heavier, I thought, than anyone on earth. Without further delay I tipped him into the river. The current seized him like a blade of grass. I watched his body turn over twice, then lost it for ever. The manager and all the pilgrims were gathered on the canopy deck near the pilot-house, chattering like excited magpies. My heartless haste drew shocked murmurs. Why they wished to leave the corpse about I cannot guess. Perhaps to embalm it. But another, more ominous murmur had reached me from below. My wood-cutter friends were equally scandalized, with rather better apparent reason, though the reason itself was utterly unacceptable. Oh, utterly! I had resolved that if anyone ate my former helmsman, it would be the fish alone. Alive he had been a distinctly second-rate steersman. Dead he might become a first-class temptation and provoke serious trouble. Besides, I wanted the wheel back. The pink-pyjama man was hopeless at it.

“The simple funeral finished, I took over immediately. At half speed we kept midstream while I listened to the others. They had abandoned all hope of Kurtz and the station. He was dead, the station burned, and so forth endlessly. The red-haired pilgrim was beside himself with delight that poor Kurtz had at least been thoroughly avenged. ‘Say! What a splendid slaughter we must have made in that bush. Eh? What do you think? Say?’ The bloodthirsty little ginger fellow actually danced. And he had almost fainted at the wounded man! I could not resist saying, ‘You certainly made a splendid quantity of smoke.’ From the shaking and flying bush-tops I knew most bullets had passed overhead. You hit nothing unless you aim and fire from the shoulder; these men shot from the hip with closed eyes. I insisted, correctly, that the steam whistle had driven the retreat. At that they forgot Kurtz and turned on me in a howl of outraged disagreement.

“Beside the wheel the manager was murmuring privately that, whatever happened, we must get well downstream before night. Then I noticed a riverside clearing in the distance and the shape of a building. ‘What is that?’ I asked. He clapped his hands in astonishment. ‘The station!’ he exclaimed. Still at half speed, I immediately steered towards it.

“My binoculars showed a hillside with scattered trees and no undergrowth. At its crest a long, rotting building stood half submerged in high grass. Great holes in its pointed roof looked black even at that distance. Jungle and forest rose behind. No fence or enclosure remained, although there had evidently been one: beside the house stood a row of six roughly trimmed, slender posts, each topped with a round carved ball. Whatever rails once joined them had gone. Forest surrounded the whole place, naturally. The riverbank lay clear. At the water’s edge a white man in a hat as broad as a cart-wheel was insistently waving his entire arm. Studying the forest margin upstream and down, I felt almost sure that human shapes moved through it. Cautiously I steamed beyond the place, stopped the engines, and let the boat drift back. The man ashore shouted for us to land. ‘We have been attacked,’ the manager screamed. ‘I know, I know. Everything’s all right,’ came the cheerful answer. ‘Come on. It’s all right. I’m glad.’

“Something about him recalled an amusing sight I had seen somewhere. While bringing the boat alongside I kept wondering whom he resembled. Then it struck me: a harlequin. His suit was probably made from brown holland, but bright patches covered it completely—blue, red, yellow, on front and back, elbows and knees. Coloured binding edged his jacket; scarlet trim ran around his trouser bottoms. In the sunshine he looked wonderfully gay and surprisingly neat, because every patch had been so skilfully sewn. His smooth, boyish face was very fair and otherwise unremarkable, with a peeling nose and small blue eyes. Smiles and frowns passed over it like sunlight and shade across a windy plain. ‘Careful, captain!’ he called. ‘A snag lodged here last night.’ What! Another one? I admit to disgraceful swearing. I had almost punctured my crippled boat to round off that delightful voyage. The harlequin lifted his small snub nose towards me, smiling. ‘English?’ he asked. ‘Are you?’ I shouted from the wheel. His smile disappeared; he shook his head as if regretting my disappointment, then brightened again. ‘Never mind!’ he called reassuringly. ‘Have we arrived in time?’ I asked. He jerked his head uphill. ‘He’s up there,’ he answered, suddenly gloomy. His face resembled an autumn sky, clouded one instant, bright the next.

“The manager and pilgrims went up to the house, armed to the teeth, and the young man boarded us. ‘I don’t care for this,’ I told him. ‘The natives are still in the trees.’ Earnestly he assured me all was well. ‘Simple people,’ he added. ‘I’m glad you arrived. Keeping them away has occupied every moment.’ ‘But you said everything was all right,’ I protested. ‘They intended no harm,’ he answered. My stare made him amend it: ‘Not exactly.’ Then, brightly: ‘My faith, this pilot-house needs cleaning!’ Immediately he advised keeping enough boiler pressure to sound the whistle if trouble arose. ‘A proper screech helps more than all your guns. They are simple people,’ he repeated. His torrent of conversation overwhelmed me. He seemed to compensate for an enormous silence and laughingly suggested that this was indeed his purpose. ‘Do you never speak with Mr. Kurtz?’ I asked. ‘One doesn’t speak with him—one listens,’ he exclaimed in stern rapture. ‘But now—’ A sweep of his arm, and he plunged into utter despair. A moment later he sprang out of it, seized both my hands, and kept shaking them while babbling: ‘Fellow sailor... honour... pleasure... delight... let me introduce myself... Russian... an arch-priest’s son... Government of Tambov... What? Tobacco! English tobacco, wonderful English tobacco! That’s brotherly indeed. Smoke? What sailor doesn’t smoke?’

“The pipe calmed him. Gradually his history emerged: he had fled school, gone to sea on a Russian vessel, deserted again, spent some time aboard English ships, and now made peace with the arch-priest. He stressed that last point. ‘When you’re young, though, you must look at things, collect experiences and ideas, broaden your mind.’ ‘Here!’ I interrupted. ‘Who can tell! It was here I found Mr. Kurtz,’ he replied with youthful solemnity and reproach. After that I held my tongue. Apparently he had talked a Dutch trading firm on the coast into supplying goods and provisions, then cheerfully set out inland, as ignorant as an infant of what might happen. For nearly two years he had roamed that river alone, separated from everyone and everything. ‘I’m older than I look. Twenty-five,’ he told me. He enjoyed recounting how he obtained his supplies. ‘At first old Van Shuyten kept telling me to go to the devil. But I stayed and talked and talked until he feared I would talk the hind-leg off his favourite dog. So he handed over some cheap goods and a few guns, hoping aloud never to see my face again. A good old Dutchman, Van Shuyten. A year ago I sent him a small shipment of ivory, so he cannot call me a petty thief when I return. I hope it reached him. Nothing else bothers me. I left firewood stacked for you. That place used to be my house. Did you notice?’

“I handed over Towson’s book. He nearly kissed me, but held himself back. Gazing at it in delight, he said, ‘My last remaining book, and I thought it lost. So many mishaps befall a man travelling alone. Sometimes a canoe overturns; sometimes the people get angry and you have to run immediately.’ He turned the pages. ‘Your notes are Russian?’ I asked. He nodded. ‘I took them for cipher,’ I told him. He laughed, then sobered. ‘Keeping those people away was very difficult.’ ‘Were they trying to kill you?’ I asked. ‘Oh, no!’ he exclaimed, then stopped himself. ‘Why attack us, then?’ I persisted. After hesitating, he answered with embarrassment, ‘They don’t want him to leave.’ ‘Don’t they?’ I asked, intrigued. His nod conveyed mystery and wisdom. ‘I tell you,’ he cried, spreading his arms and fixing me with perfectly round little blue eyes, ‘that man has broadened my mind.’”

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: “Astonished, I stared at him. There he stood in his motley clothes, eager and fantastic, like a runaway from a company of mimes. That he existed at all seemed improbable, inexplicable, bewildering. He was a riddle without an answer. How had he survived, travelled so far, stayed there? Why did he not vanish on the spot? ‘I went a bit farther,’ he said, ‘and then a bit farther again, until I had gone so far I cannot imagine getting back. Never mind. There is time. I’ll manage. You must take Kurtz away quickly, quickly, I tell you.’ Youth cast its glamour over his many-coloured rags, his poverty and loneliness, the underlying desolation of his pointless wandering. For months, for years, his life had not been worth a day’s purchase. Yet here he was, gallantly and thoughtlessly alive, apparently indestructible through youth and heedless daring alone. I found myself drawn towards admiration, almost envy. Glamour drove him forward and protected him. Surely he asked the wilderness for nothing except room to breathe and keep moving. He needed simply to exist and advance, taking the greatest risks and suffering the greatest deprivation possible. If pure adventure, without calculation or practical purpose, ever mastered a human being, it mastered this patched young fellow. I nearly envied that clear, modest flame within him. It seemed to have burned away all concern for himself so completely that, even while he spoke, you forgot that the man before you had lived through these events. His devotion to Kurtz I did not envy. He had never reflected on it; it had arrived, and he welcomed it with eager fatalism. To me it seemed, in every respect, the most dangerous thing he had yet encountered.

“Their meeting had been inevitable, like two ships lying becalmed nearby until their sides eventually rubbed together. Presumably Kurtz needed a listener. Once, while camped in the forest, they talked through the night—or, more probably, Kurtz talked. The memory carried the young man away. ‘We discussed everything. I forgot sleep existed. The whole night seemed less than an hour. Everything! Everything!... Love as well.’ ‘Ah, so he spoke of love!’ I said, amused. ‘Not what you imagine,’ he protested almost fiercely. ‘Love in general. He showed me things—things.’

“His arms flew upwards. We were standing on deck, and the wood-cutters’ headman, resting nearby, turned his heavy, shining eyes towards him. I glanced around. For some reason I cannot explain, that country, that river, that jungle, even the vault of burning sky, had never before looked so hopelessly dark, so closed to human understanding, so merciless towards human frailty. Never before, I assure you. ‘And naturally you have stayed with him ever since?’ I asked.

“Quite the opposite. Many circumstances had repeatedly separated them. He proudly told me he had nursed Kurtz through two illnesses, speaking as one might of a dangerous exploit. Usually, though, Kurtz wandered alone far inside the forest. ‘Often I arrived at this station and waited day after day for him to appear,’ he said. ‘Ah, sometimes the wait was worthwhile!’ ‘What was he doing? Exploring?’ I asked. ‘Yes, certainly.’ He had discovered a large number of villages, and a lake as well. The young man did not know exactly in which direction that lake lay; enquiring too closely into Kurtz’s activities was a dangerous business. Mostly, however, he went out for ivory. ‘But by then he had nothing left to exchange,’ I objected. Looking away, he replied, ‘There are still plenty of cartridges.’ ‘In plain language, he raided the country,’ I said. A nod. ‘Surely not alone!’ He muttered about the villages around the lake. ‘So Kurtz persuaded the tribe to follow him?’ I suggested. He shifted uneasily. ‘They worshipped him.’ His tone was so remarkable that I studied him closely. The mixture of eagerness and unwillingness with which he discussed Kurtz was curious. Kurtz filled his existence, possessed his thoughts, governed his feelings. ‘What else could you expect?’ he burst out. ‘He arrived among them with thunder and lightning. They had never seen anything similar. Terrible, very terrible. He could be terrifying. You cannot judge Mr. Kurtz by ordinary standards. No, no, no! To give you some notion, I will tell you that once he intended to shoot me too. But I do not judge him.’ ‘Shoot you!’ I exclaimed. ‘Why?’ ‘I had a little ivory given me by the chief of the village near my house. I used to hunt game for them. Kurtz wanted it and refused to listen to reason. He said he would shoot me unless I handed it over and left the country. He could do it, he felt like doing it, and nothing on earth could prevent him killing anyone he pleased. That was true enough. I gave him the ivory. What did I care! But I never left. No, I could not abandon him. Naturally I took care until we became friendly again for a while. Then came his second illness. Afterwards I had to stay out of sight, but I did not mind. He spent most of his time in those lakeside villages. When he returned to the river he sometimes liked me, and sometimes I needed to be cautious. He suffered terribly. He loathed all this, yet somehow could not escape. Whenever possible I begged him to leave while there was time, offering to accompany him. He would agree, then stay, set out hunting ivory again, disappear for weeks, lose himself among those people—lose himself, you understand.’ ‘Why! He is mad,’ I said. The young man protested angrily. Mr. Kurtz could not be mad. Had I heard him speaking just two days earlier, I would never suggest it.... During this conversation I had raised my binoculars and was examining the shore, tracing the forest boundary beside and behind the house. Knowing there were people in that silent bush, silent as the ruined hillside house, troubled me. Nature’s face revealed nothing of the astonishing story conveyed less in narrative than in sorrowful exclamations, shrugs, broken phrases, and hints ending with deep sighs. The forest remained expressionless as a mask, heavy as a prison’s shut door, with its concealed knowledge, patient expectation, inaccessible silence. The Russian explained that Kurtz had only recently returned to the river, bringing the lake tribe’s entire fighting force. For several months he had been absent—receiving worship, I suppose—then appeared unexpectedly, apparently intending a raid across the river or farther downstream. Clearly the appetite for ivory had overcome the—what shall I call them?—less material ambitions. Then he had suddenly grown much worse. ‘I heard he was helpless, so I came up and risked it,’ said the Russian. ‘He is very ill, terribly ill.’ I turned my glasses towards the house. No life showed there. The ruined roof, the long mud wall above the grass, and three small square window openings, each a different size, seemed within arm’s reach. A sharp movement brought one surviving fence post leaping into view. You remember those attempts at decoration I noticed from afar, remarkable amid the ruin. Suddenly seeing one close, I recoiled as though struck. Then I carefully examined each post and understood my mistake. The rounded tops were symbols, not ornaments: expressive, perplexing, startling, disturbing. Food for thought and for vultures, had any been watching overhead; certainly for industrious ants willing to climb. The heads on those stakes would have impressed still more had their faces not turned towards the house. Only the first I saw faced me. Do not imagine I was as horrified as you might expect. My recoil was simple surprise. I had anticipated a wooden knob. Deliberately I returned to the first head. Black, dry, shrunken, eyes closed, it seemed asleep atop its pole. Its shrivelled lips exposed a narrow white line of teeth, making it smile endlessly at some everlasting, merry dream of that eternal sleep.

“I am revealing no secrets of the trade. Indeed, the manager later claimed that Mr. Kurtz’s methods had ruined the district. On that question I offer no judgment. But I want you to understand clearly that keeping those heads there served no profitable purpose. They showed only his inability to restrain the satisfaction of his various appetites, some lack within him, some small necessity that, when urgently required, could not be found beneath his splendid eloquence. Whether he recognized that deficiency himself I cannot tell. I believe the knowledge reached him finally, but only at the very end. The wilderness, however, discovered it early and took terrible revenge for that fantastic invasion. I think it whispered truths about himself that he had never known, things he had never even imagined before consulting that immense solitude. The whisper fascinated him irresistibly. It echoed loudly inside him because his centre was hollow.... I lowered the binoculars. The head, which had seemed near enough for me to speak to, instantly sprang away into a distance I could not reach.

“Kurtz’s admirer looked rather dismayed. Quickly and indistinctly, he assured me he had not dared remove those—let us call them—symbols. The natives did not frighten him; they would do nothing without Kurtz’s command. His authority was extraordinary. Their encampments surrounded the station, and chiefs visited daily. They would crawl.... ‘I want no account of the ceremonies for approaching Mr. Kurtz,’ I shouted. Strange that I felt such details would be harder to endure than the heads drying beneath his windows. After all, those were merely a savage spectacle. I seemed to have leapt into some unlit realm of intricate horrors, where plain, uncomplicated savagery offered relief, something obviously entitled to exist in daylight. The young man stared in surprise. He apparently never considered that Kurtz was no idol to me. He forgot I had heard none of those magnificent monologues on love, justice, the conduct of life, or whatever their subjects were. As for crawling before Kurtz, he crawled as thoroughly as the most complete savage. I did not understand the circumstances, he insisted. Those were rebels’ heads. My laughter shocked him profoundly. Rebels! What new label would come next? First enemies, then criminals, then workers; now rebels. On their sticks, those rebellious heads looked thoroughly subdued. ‘You have no idea how this life tests a man like Kurtz,’ his last disciple cried. ‘And you?’ I asked. ‘I! I! I am an ordinary man, without great thoughts. I ask nothing of anyone. How can you compare me with...?’ Feeling overwhelmed his speech, and abruptly he broke down. ‘I cannot understand,’ he groaned. ‘I have tried my hardest to keep him living. That is enough. None of this was my doing. I have no special abilities. For months there has been no medicine, no suitable food for an invalid. They abandoned him disgracefully. Such a man, with such ideas. Disgracefully! Disgracefully! I—I have not slept for ten nights...’

“His voice faded into the calm of the evening. While we talked, the forest’s long shadows had crept downhill and travelled well beyond the ruined hut and its symbolic row of stakes. Darkness covered them all, although we below still stood in sunlight. Beside the clearing the broad river gleamed with a motionless, dazzling brilliance, while shadowed bends lay murky both upstream and down. Not a living soul appeared anywhere along the shore. No rustling came from the bushes.

“Abruptly a group of men appeared around the house’s corner, as though rising straight out of the earth. In a tight formation they pushed through waist-high grass, carrying a makeshift stretcher in their midst. A cry immediately rose over the empty landscape, piercing the still air like a sharp arrow aimed straight into the land’s heart. As if under a spell, the dark, thoughtful forest poured streams of people, naked people, into the clearing. They carried spears, bows, and shields, their eyes fierce and their movements wild. The shrubs shook and the grass waved for a little while. Then everything settled into attentive, motionless watchfulness.

“‘Unless he says the proper thing, we are finished,’ the Russian said beside me. The stretcher party had also halted halfway to the boat, seemingly turned to stone. Above the bearers’ shoulders the man on it sat up, long and thin, one arm raised. ‘Let us hope that someone so eloquent about love in general can find a particular reason to spare us now,’ I said. I bitterly resented our ridiculous peril, as if dependence on that dreadful ghost were a humiliation forced upon us. No sound reached me. Through the glasses I saw the thin arm commanding, the jaw moving, the eyes shining darkly in the depths of a bony head that nodded with grotesque jerks. Kurtz: that means short in German, doesn’t it? His name was as truthful as everything else about his life and death. He seemed seven feet long at least. His covering slipped aside, revealing his body as pitiful and frightening as a corpse emerging from its shroud. I could see the ribcage moving and the arm bones waving. An image of death carved in ancient ivory seemed to have come alive and to be threatening a motionless crowd of dark, polished bronze figures. His mouth opened wide. He looked weirdly ravenous, as though wishing to swallow all the air, the earth, the men before him. A deep voice faintly reached us; he must have been shouting. Suddenly he dropped back. The bearers staggered forward, shaking the stretcher. Almost simultaneously I saw the savages disappearing without visible retreat, as though the forest that had expelled them now drew them back in one long breath.

“Pilgrims following the stretcher carried his weapons: two shot-guns, a heavy rifle, and a light revolver-carbine, the thunderbolts of that miserable Jupiter. Walking beside his head, the manager bent and murmured over him. They installed him in a small cabin with barely space for a bed and one or two camp-stools. We had delivered his overdue mail, and ripped envelopes and opened letters covered the bed. His hand wandered weakly through them. The burning eyes and his calmly languid expression struck me. It was more than illness’s exhaustion. He appeared free of pain. The shadow looked satisfied and peaceful, as though it had temporarily exhausted every possible emotion.

“He stirred a letter and looked straight at me. ‘I am glad,’ he said. Someone had written about me; those special recommendations had surfaced again. The sheer volume he produced without effort, scarcely moving his lips, astonished me. A voice! A voice! Low, deep, resonant, from a man who seemed unable even to whisper. Yet enough strength remained, artificially sustained no doubt, almost to destroy us, as you will soon hear.

“Without a sound the manager appeared in the doorway. I immediately went out, and he closed the curtain behind me. Under the pilgrims’ curious scrutiny, the Russian stood staring ashore. I looked where he was looking.

“Far away, dark figures moved indistinctly against the forest’s sombre edge. Closer to the river, two bronze figures rested on long spears in the sun, wearing fantastic headdresses of spotted skins, warlike yet still as statues. Along the bright bank, from right towards left, advanced the wild, splendid apparition of a woman.

“Her steps were measured and proud beneath striped, fringed cloths. Barbarous ornaments faintly jingled and flashed. She held her head high, her hair fashioned like a helmet. Brass leggings reached her knees, brass-wire gauntlets her elbows. A crimson mark showed on her tawny cheek, and countless glass-bead necklaces circled her neck. Odd objects, charms, gifts from witch-men, hung about her, trembling and shining as she walked. She must have worn several elephant tusks’ worth. Savage and superb, magnificently wild-eyed, she moved with a deliberate majesty that carried something ominous. In the hush suddenly covering that sorrowful country, the immense wilderness, that colossal body of fertile, mysterious life, seemed to contemplate her as an image of its own dark, passionate soul.

“When she reached the steamer’s position she stopped and turned towards us. Her shadow stretched to the water. Her fierce, tragic face held wild grief and speechless pain, mingled with fear of some struggling purpose not yet fully formed. Motionless, she watched us, seeming, like the wilderness, to brood upon an unreadable intention. After a full minute she stepped forward. Metal jingled softly and flashed yellow, fringes swayed, and she halted as though courage had deserted her. The young man beside me growled; behind me the pilgrims murmured. Her unwavering gaze embraced us all as if keeping it steady were a matter of life itself. Suddenly she spread her bare arms and thrust them rigidly overhead, apparently seized by an uncontrollable longing to touch the sky. At the same instant shadows raced across the ground and swept around the river, enclosing the steamer in a dark embrace. An imposing silence hung upon everything.
“Slowly she turned away and continued along the bank into the bushes on our left. Just once her eyes flashed back towards us through the dim undergrowth; then she was gone.

“‘Had she tried to board us, I believe I would have shot at her,’ the patched man said nervously. ‘For two weeks I risked my life daily keeping her outside the house. Once she got in and made a tremendous fuss over the scraps I had taken from the storeroom to repair my clothes. I wasn’t decently dressed. At least that must have been it: she raged at Kurtz for an hour, pointing towards me occasionally. This tribe’s dialect is beyond me. Luckily, I think he was too ill that day to care, or trouble would have followed. I cannot understand.... No, it is beyond me. Well, everything is over now.’

“Then Kurtz’s deep voice sounded behind the curtain. ‘Save me! You mean save the ivory. Don’t tell me otherwise. Save _me!_ I have had to save you. Now you disrupt my plans. Sick! Sick! Not nearly as sick as you hope to believe. Never mind. I shall carry out my ideas yet. I shall return and show you what can be achieved. Your petty trading notions obstruct me. I shall come back. I....’

“The manager emerged and honoured me by slipping his hand under my arm and drawing me aside. ‘Very weak, very weak,’ he said. He thought a sigh necessary but failed to sustain the sorrowful manner. ‘We have done everything possible, have we not? Still, the fact remains that Mr. Kurtz has injured the Company more than he has helped it. He failed to realize the time was not right for forceful action. Caution, caution: that is my principle. Caution is still necessary. For a while the district is shut to us. Deplorable! Trade in general will suffer. Certainly there is an exceptional quantity of ivory, mostly fossil. We must preserve that whatever happens. But consider our precarious position. Why? Unsound methods.’ Looking ashore, I asked, ‘You call this “unsound method?”’ ‘Of course,’ he answered heatedly. ‘Don’t you?’... Eventually I murmured, ‘No method whatsoever.’ ‘Precisely,’ he said triumphantly. ‘I foresaw it. A total absence of judgment, which duty requires me to report to the proper authorities.’ ‘That fellow, what’s his name, the brickmaker,’ I said, ‘can compose an entertaining report for you.’ For a moment he looked baffled. Never, I thought, had I breathed such a vile atmosphere. Mentally I turned to Kurtz for relief, actual relief. ‘Nevertheless, I consider Mr. Kurtz a remarkable man,’ I said emphatically. He started, gave me a heavy look, and replied softly, ‘He _was_.’ Then he turned away. My brief favour had ended. Now I was classed with Kurtz, a supporter of methods whose moment had not arrived. I was unsound! Ah! Even a choice between nightmares was something.

“Really I had turned towards the wilderness. Kurtz himself, I willingly admitted, was practically buried already. For a moment I felt buried too, in a vast grave containing unspeakable secrets. An unbearable pressure weighed on my chest: damp earth’s smell, the unseen nearness of triumphant decay, a night whose darkness nothing could pierce.... The Russian touched my shoulder. His muttering, stumbling words concerned ‘brother seaman—couldn’t conceal—knowledge of matters that would affect Mr. Kurtz’s reputation.’ I waited. Evidently Kurtz was not in the grave for him. I suspect he counted Kurtz among the immortals. At last I said, ‘Well! Out with it. As it happens, I am his friend, after a fashion.’

“With considerable ceremony he explained that, had we not belonged to ‘the same profession,’ he would have kept his knowledge private regardless of consequences. ‘He suspected these white men actively wished him harm, and—’ ‘Quite right,’ I interrupted, remembering an overheard conversation. ‘The manager believes you should be hanged.’ His alarm initially amused me. ‘Then I ought to slip away quietly,’ he said earnestly. ‘I can do nothing more for Kurtz. They would soon invent a pretext. What could stop them? A military post lies three hundred miles away.’ ‘Indeed,’ I replied, ‘perhaps departure would be wise, if you have friends among the local savages.’ ‘Many. They are simple people, and I ask for nothing.’ He bit his lip before continuing. ‘I wish these white men no harm. Naturally my concern was Mr. Kurtz’s reputation. But you are a fellow sailor, and—’ Eventually I answered, ‘All right. His reputation is safe in my hands.’ I did not realize how true that would prove.

“Lowering his voice, he disclosed that Kurtz had ordered the attack on us. ‘Sometimes he could not bear the thought of removal, and then again.... These matters are beyond me. I am an ordinary man.
