He hoped to frighten you off, make you abandon the journey believing him dead. I could not prevent it. The past month has been terrible.’ ‘Very well,’ I said. ‘We have him safely now.’ ‘Ye-e-es,’ he muttered without much conviction. ‘Thank you. I shall remain watchful,’ I told him. ‘But discreet, eh?’ he pleaded anxiously. ‘His reputation would suffer terribly if anyone here—’ Solemnly I promised complete silence. ‘A canoe and three black fellows are waiting nearby. I’m leaving. Could you spare some Martini-Henry cartridges?’ I could, and secretly supplied them. Winking, he took a handful of my tobacco. ‘Between sailors, you understand. Fine English tobacco.’ At the pilot-house doorway he turned back. ‘Any spare shoes, by chance?’ Raising a foot, he said, ‘Look.’ Knotted strings held bare soles beneath his feet like sandals. I found an old pair, which he admired before tucking them under his left arm. Cartridges bulged in a bright-red pocket; from the dark-blue one protruded ‘Towson’s Inquiry,’ and so forth. He apparently considered himself magnificently equipped to confront the wilderness again. ‘Ah! Never, never shall I meet another such man. You should have heard his poetry recitations. His own poetry, he told me. Poetry!’ He rolled his eyes in remembered delight. ‘Oh, how he broadened my mind!’ ‘Good-bye,’ I said. He shook my hand and disappeared into darkness. Sometimes I wonder whether I truly saw him, whether meeting such a phenomenon was possible!...

“Waking soon after midnight, I remembered his warning and its suggestion of danger. Beneath the stars that danger felt real enough to make me get up and look carefully around. A large fire burned on the hillside, flickering upon a crooked corner of the station building. An agent and a small guard of our black men, armed for the purpose, watched over the ivory. Deep inside the forest, shifting red lights seemed to rise and sink from the ground among confused, column-like shapes of intense darkness. They marked the exact position of the camp where Kurtz’s worshippers kept their troubled vigil. A large drum’s monotonous beat filled the air with muffled impacts and persistent vibrations. From the forest’s flat black wall came the steady drone of many men, each chanting some strange incantation to himself, like bees humming inside a hive. It had an oddly drugging effect on my half-awakened senses. I think I dozed leaning on the rail until a sudden eruption of screams, an overwhelming release of pent-up, mysterious frenzy, roused me in bewildered amazement. It ended abruptly. The low drone resumed, like a soothing silence made audible. Casually I looked inside the little cabin. Its light burned, but Kurtz was no longer there.

“Had I trusted my eyes, I think I would have shouted. Initially I could not: it seemed impossible. Pure, empty fear utterly unnerved me, an abstract terror unrelated to any recognizable physical threat. Its overwhelming force came from—how can I describe it?—a moral shock, as though something monstrous, unbearable to thought and hateful to the soul, had suddenly been forced upon me. Naturally this lasted only a fraction of a second. Then ordinary mortal danger returned: the possibility of an imminent attack, a massacre, some such recognizable event. That prospect actually welcomed and steadied me. It calmed me so thoroughly, in fact, that I gave no alarm.

“An agent slept in a deck chair three feet away, buttoned inside his ulster. The cries had not disturbed his faint snoring. I let him sleep and jumped ashore. I did not betray Kurtz. It was decreed that I should never betray him, written that I must remain faithful to the nightmare I had chosen. I wanted to confront that shadow alone. Even now I cannot explain why I so jealously refused to share the peculiar darkness of that experience with another person.

“On the bank I immediately found a broad track through the grass. I remember triumphantly telling myself, ‘He cannot walk. He must be crawling on all fours. I have him.’ Dew wet the grass. I strode quickly forward, fists clenched. Perhaps I vaguely intended to jump on him and beat him. I do not know; idiotic thoughts filled me. The old knitting woman with her cat intruded on my memory. What an improper figure to occupy the other end of such a business. I pictured pilgrims lined up, shooting into the sky with Winchesters held at their hips. I imagined never reaching the boat again, living unarmed and solitary among the trees into old age. Nonsense of that sort, you understand. I also remember mistaking the drumbeats for my heart and feeling pleased at its steady calm.

“Still I followed the track, then paused to listen. The night was remarkably clear, a dark-blue expanse sparkling with stars and dew, with black shapes standing utterly motionless. Something seemed to move ahead. That night I felt strangely certain of everything. I actually left the path and ran in a broad half-circle, chuckling to myself, I believe, to intercept the movement I thought I had seen—if I had seen anything. I was outflanking Kurtz as though playing a childhood game.

“I found him. Had he not heard me, I would have tripped over him, but he rose just in time. Tall, pale, unsteady, indistinct, he lifted himself like vapour breathing from the ground and swayed silently before me. Behind me fires glimmered between trunks and many voices murmured. I had neatly intercepted him. Face to face, though, I seemed to regain my senses and recognize the true danger. It was far from ended. What if he shouted? He could barely stand, but his voice still possessed considerable force. ‘Go away. Hide,’ he ordered in that deep tone. It was dreadful. I glanced back. The nearest fire lay within thirty yards. A black figure rose and crossed the glow, long legs striding, long arms waving. Horns, apparently antelope horns, stood on its head. Some sorcerer or witch-man, surely; it looked devilish enough. ‘Do you understand what you are doing?’ I whispered. ‘Perfectly,’ he answered, raising his voice on that word. It sounded distant yet loud, like a call through a speaking-trumpet. If he raises an alarm, I thought, we are lost. Clearly fists offered no solution, quite apart from my natural reluctance to strike that Shadow, that wandering, tormented creature. ‘You will be lost,’ I told him, ‘completely lost.’ Sometimes inspiration flashes upon you. I had chosen the right words, although he could hardly have been more irretrievably lost than at that instant, when our intimacy began: an intimacy that would last to the end and beyond it.

“‘My plans were immense,’ he murmured uncertainly. ‘Yes,’ I replied, ‘but shout and I shall break your head with—’ No stone or stick lay near. ‘I shall strangle you outright,’ I amended. ‘I stood on the verge of great achievements,’ he pleaded, with a yearning that chilled my blood. ‘And now this stupid scoundrel—’ ‘Whatever happens, success in Europe awaits you,’ I assured him firmly. You understand, I had no wish to strangle him. Practically speaking it would have achieved very little. I was attempting to break the wilderness’s heavy, speechless spell. It seemed to draw him towards its merciless breast by stirring forgotten brutal instincts and memories of monstrous appetites satisfied. This alone, I felt certain, had brought him to the forest’s edge, towards bush, firelight, pulsing drums, and droning incantations. It alone had lured his lawless soul outside the limits of permitted ambition. The horror of my position, you see, was less the chance of being clubbed—though I felt that danger keenly—than confronting someone to whom neither lofty nor humble appeals meant anything. Like the niggers, I could invoke only him, himself, his own exalted, incredible degradation. I knew nothing stood above or beneath him. He had kicked himself free of the earth. Damn him! He had smashed the earth itself to pieces. He was alone, and facing him I could not tell whether solid ground supported me or I floated in air. I have repeated what we said, the actual phrases, but to what purpose? Ordinary daily words, familiar vague sounds exchanged throughout waking life. Yet behind them, to me, lay the terrible suggestiveness of dream-speech, of words uttered in nightmares. Soul! If anyone has wrestled with a soul, I have. Nor was my opponent intellectually insane. Believe it or not, his intelligence remained clear, hideously concentrated on himself, but clear. That gave me my only chance, apart from killing him immediately, an inconvenient course because of the inevitable noise. His soul, however, was mad. Alone in the wilderness it had examined itself and, by heavens! had gone mad. For my sins, I suppose, I was forced to undergo the ordeal of examining it too. Nothing eloquent could have withered faith in humanity more than his final eruption of honesty. He fought himself as well; I witnessed and heard it. Here was the unimaginable mystery of a soul without restraint, faith, or fear, blindly struggling against itself. I stayed reasonably composed. But after finally laying him on the couch I wiped my brow while my legs shook as though I had carried half a ton downhill. In fact I had merely supported him, his bony arm around my neck. He weighed scarcely more than a child.

“We departed at noon the next day. All along I had felt acutely the crowd hidden beyond the trees. Now it poured out again, filling the clearing and covering the hillside with naked bronze bodies, breathing and trembling. I steamed a little upstream, then turned down. Two thousand eyes tracked our manoeuvres: a fierce river-demon splashing and pounding, lashing water with its terrible tail and breathing black smoke. Before the foremost rank, three men restlessly strutted along the river, covered head to foot in bright-red earth. As we passed again they faced us, stamped, nodded horned heads, and swayed scarlet bodies. They shook towards the demon a bunch of black feathers, a mangy hide with a dangling tail, and something resembling a dried gourd. At intervals they shouted together extraordinary strings of words unlike any human language. The crowd’s deep murmurs, abruptly interrupted, resembled responses in a satanic litany.

“We had moved Kurtz to the pilot-house for better air. From the couch he stared through the open shutter. The crowd stirred and parted, and the woman with tawny cheeks and helmet-like hair rushed to the river’s very edge. She stretched out her hands and shouted. The whole wild multitude echoed her in a roaring chorus, its rapid, distinct syllables tumbling out breathlessly.
“‘Can you understand what they are saying?’ I asked.

“He continued staring beyond me with burning, yearning eyes, longing and hatred mingled in his face. He gave no reply. A smile of unreadable meaning touched his bloodless lips, which then jerked violently. ‘Do I not?’ he finally gasped, slowly, as though some supernatural force had dragged the words out of him.

“Seeing the pilgrims below taking out their rifles with the eager air of men expecting a pleasant entertainment, I pulled the whistle cord. Its sudden scream sent utter terror through that tightly packed mass of bodies. ‘Don’t! Don’t scare them off,’ someone on deck complained mournfully. I pulled the cord and sounded the whistle again and again. They scattered, ran, jumped, crouched, swerved, dodging the airborne terror of the noise. The three red men dropped flat, face down along the shore, as though bullets had killed them. Only the superb, barbarous woman did not flinch at all. Tragically she extended her bare arms after us across the darkly glittering river.
“Then the fools on the lower deck began their little amusement, and gun smoke blotted out everything I could see.

“The brown water hurried from the heart of darkness, carrying us seaward twice as fast as we had travelled upstream. Kurtz’s life hurried too, ebbing from his heart into the sea of time that yields to no one. The manager was perfectly tranquil. Nothing essential troubled him now. A satisfied, all-embracing glance took in both of us: the ‘affair’ had ended as well as anyone could wish. Soon, I saw, I would be the sole survivor of the ‘unsound method’ party. The pilgrims regarded me unfavourably. In a sense they had already counted me among the dead. Strange how readily I accepted this unexpected alliance, this forced choice of nightmares in a dark country invaded by petty, grasping ghosts.

“Kurtz kept talking. A voice! A voice! Its depth and resonance lasted to the end, outliving his strength and concealing his heart’s barren darkness beneath splendid folds of language. How he fought! How he fought! Shadowy visions haunted his exhausted brain’s wastelands: wealth and glory circling obediently around his indestructible talent for noble, elevated expression. My Intended, my station, my career, my ideas: these supplied his occasional lofty sentiments. The ghost of the earlier Kurtz haunted the bedside of the empty fraud soon to be buried in primeval soil. Both a devilish love and an unearthly hatred of the mysteries he had entered struggled to possess that soul, glutted with primitive feelings yet hungry for counterfeit fame, false distinction, every outward sign of achievement and authority.

“At times his childishness was contemptible. Returning from some dreadful Nowhere where he meant to perform great deeds, he wanted kings waiting at railway-stations to greet him. ‘Demonstrate something genuinely profitable in yourself, and recognition of your ability will know no bounds,’ he would say. ‘Always attend to the motives, of course. Correct motives, always.’ The long reaches and monotonous bends, each indistinguishable from the last, passed us with their multitude of ancient trees. Patiently the trees watched this dirty fragment of another world, heralding change, conquest, commerce, massacres, blessings. I watched ahead and steered. One day Kurtz abruptly said, ‘Shut the shutter. I cannot endure the sight.’ I obeyed. Silence followed. Then he cried to the hidden wilderness, ‘Oh, I will wrench your heart yet!’

“As I had expected, we broke down and stopped for repairs at an island’s upstream end. That delay first disturbed Kurtz’s confidence. One morning he handed me papers and a photograph bundled together with a shoelace. ‘Guard these for me,’ he said. ‘That poisonous fool’—the manager—‘might search my boxes when I am not watching.’ In the afternoon I found him stretched on his back, eyes shut. I was quietly withdrawing when he murmured, ‘Live rightly, die, die...’ I stopped to listen; nothing followed. Was he practising a speech in sleep, or recalling a phrase from a newspaper article? He had contributed to newspapers and intended to resume, ‘for the furthering of my ideas. It’s a duty.’

“His darkness could not be penetrated. Watching him felt like peering down at someone lying at the foot of a precipice never reached by sunlight. But little time remained for him. I helped the engine-driver dismantle leaking cylinders, straighten a bent connecting-rod, and perform similar jobs. Rust, metal filings, nuts, bolts, spanners, hammers, ratchet-drills: I lived among a hellish jumble of objects I detest because I handle them poorly. Fortunately we had a small forge aboard, which I tended. I laboured wearily in that miserable scrap-heap, except when shaking made standing impossible.

“One evening I entered with a candle and was startled by his slightly trembling voice: ‘I am lying here in the dark waiting for death.’ The flame stood less than a foot from his eyes. I forced out, ‘Oh, nonsense!’ and remained above him as though rooted there.

“Never before had I seen a face change as his did, and I hope never to witness anything similar again. It did not move me; it fascinated me. A veil seemed torn apart. On that ivory face appeared dark pride, merciless power, cowardly terror, and a hopeless despair of terrible intensity. In that supreme instant of total understanding, did he relive every desire, temptation, and surrender of his life? At some image or vision he cried in a whisper, twice, with scarcely more than a breath:
“‘The horror! The horror!’

“I blew out the candle and left the cabin. The pilgrims were eating in the mess-room, and I took my seat opposite the manager. He raised his eyes in a questioning look, which I managed to ignore. Serenely he leaned back, his peculiar smile sealing the unspoken depths of his pettiness. A continuous shower of tiny flies streamed onto the lamp and tablecloth, onto our hands and faces. Suddenly the manager’s boy thrust his insolent black head through the doorway and announced with biting contempt:
“‘Mistah Kurtz—he dead.’

“Every pilgrim hurried out to look. I stayed with my dinner, thereby earning, I believe, a reputation for brutal indifference. I ate little, though. A lamp burned in the room: light, you understand. Outside lay that dreadful, dreadful darkness. I never again approached the remarkable man who had judged his soul’s adventures on earth. The voice had departed. What else had there been? Naturally I know that the following day the pilgrims put something into a muddy grave.
“Soon afterwards they came very close to burying me too.

“As you see, though, I did not immediately follow Kurtz. I remained, to dream the nightmare through to its conclusion and prove my loyalty once again. Fate. My own fate! Life is a curious business, that mysterious combination of pitiless reasoning and purposeless ends. At best you gain some self-knowledge too late, a harvest of regrets that cannot die. I have struggled with death. No contest could be less exciting. It happens in an intangible greyness, with nothing beneath your feet or around you, no witnesses, noise, or glory, no fierce wish to win or great dread of losing. A sickly atmosphere of lukewarm doubt surrounds it. You scarcely believe in your own claim, and believe even less in your opponent’s. If that is final wisdom, life presents a greater puzzle than some imagine. A hair’s breadth separated me from my last chance to pronounce upon it, and humiliatingly I found I probably had nothing to say. That is why I insist on Kurtz’s distinction. He possessed something to say and said it. Having peered over the edge myself, I understand better that stare which missed the candle flame yet encompassed the universe, which pierced the hearts beating throughout darkness. He had summed up and passed judgment. ‘The horror!’ A remarkable man. After all, some belief expressed itself there: frankness, conviction, a trembling whisper of rebellion, the terrible face of truth momentarily glimpsed, desire and hatred strangely intermingled. What I remember most clearly is not my own extremity, that shapeless greyness full of bodily pain and careless contempt for the passing of everything, even pain itself. No! I seem to have lived through his extremity. True, he took the final step over the edge; I was allowed to withdraw my hesitant foot. Perhaps that makes the entire difference. Perhaps all wisdom, truth, and honesty compress into that immeasurably brief moment when we cross into the invisible. Perhaps! I prefer to believe my own final verdict would have risen above indifferent contempt. His cry was better, far better: an affirmation, a moral victory purchased through countless defeats, appalling fears, appalling gratifications. Yet a victory! That explains my loyalty to Kurtz until the end and afterwards, when much later I heard, not his voice itself, but his splendid eloquence echoed from a soul as transparently pure as a cliff of crystal.

“They did not bury me, no. But one stretch remains hazy in my memory, recalled with shuddering wonder like a journey through an unimaginable world without hope or desire. Back in the sepulchral city, I resented the people rushing through its streets to steal a little money from one another, swallow their vile cooking and unhealthy beer, dream their small, foolish dreams. They trespassed on my thoughts. Their supposed understanding of life seemed an irritating fraud, since I felt certain they could not possibly know what I knew. Their manner was merely that of ordinary people attending to business in perfect security. Yet it offended me as folly brazenly flaunting itself before a danger it cannot grasp. I had little wish to enlighten them, but struggled not to laugh into those stupidly self-important faces. I was probably still unwell. With various affairs to settle, I staggered about the streets grinning bitterly at thoroughly respectable citizens. My conduct was indefensible, I admit, but my temperature rarely stayed normal then. My dear aunt’s efforts to ‘nurse up my strength’ missed the point. Strength needed no nursing; imagination needed calming. I kept Kurtz’s papers, unsure what to do with them. His mother had recently died, attended, I was told, by his Intended. One day a clean-shaven visitor with an official air and gold-rimmed spectacles asked about what he chose to call certain ‘documents.’ First indirect, his questions became smoothly insistent. This did not surprise me: out there I had quarrelled twice with the manager over the same subject. I had refused to surrender the smallest scrap, and gave the spectacled visitor the same answer. Finally he grew threatening, heatedly asserting the Company’s ownership of every piece of information concerning its ‘territories.’ ‘Mr. Kurtz must have possessed extensive, exceptional knowledge of unexplored regions,’ he argued, ‘given his abilities and the regrettable circumstances surrounding him. Therefore—’ I assured him that, however extensive, the knowledge had nothing to do with commercial or administrative questions. Then he appealed to science. ‘It would be an incalculable loss if,’ and so on. I offered the ‘Suppression of Savage Customs’ report, with its postscriptum removed. He seized it eagerly, but ended by sniffing in disdain. ‘We were entitled to expect something different,’ he remarked. ‘Expect nothing further,’ I said. ‘The rest is private correspondence.’ Threatening legal action, he departed for good. Two days later another man appeared, introducing himself as Kurtz’s cousin and demanding every detail of his beloved relative’s death. Incidentally he explained that Kurtz was essentially a great musician. ‘He had the makings of an enormous success,’ said this visitor, an organist, I think, with long grey hair over a greasy collar. I had no reason to disbelieve him. Even now I cannot name Kurtz’s profession, if he had one, or identify his greatest talent. I thought him a painter who wrote for newspapers, or a journalist who painted. Even the cousin, taking snuff as we spoke, could not define what he had been. A universal genius: on that we agreed. The old man then blew his nose loudly in a large cotton handkerchief and left in aged agitation, carrying family letters and insignificant notes. Finally a journalist arrived to enquire after his ‘dear colleague.’ He believed politics ‘on the popular side’ was Kurtz’s natural field. With bushy straight eyebrows, short bristling hair, and an eyeglass on a wide ribbon, he became expansive and admitted that Kurtz could scarcely write at all. ‘But heavens! What a speaker. He electrified public meetings. He had faith, you understand, the faith. He could persuade himself of anything whatever. He would have led an extreme party magnificently.’ ‘Which party?’ I asked. ‘Any party. He was an—an—extremist.’ Did I agree? I did. Curiosity suddenly flashing, he asked whether I knew ‘what it was that had induced him to go out there?’ ‘Yes,’ I said, and handed over the famous Report for publication if he wished. He rapidly scanned it, muttering, decided ‘it would do,’ and carried off his loot.

“At last only a thin bundle of letters and the girl’s photograph remained. She seemed beautiful, or rather her expression did. Sunlight too can be made to lie, I know, yet no contrivance of pose or lighting seemed capable of producing that delicate truthfulness in her face. She appeared prepared to listen without suspicion, mental reservation, or concern for herself. I decided to return the portrait and letters personally. Curiosity? Yes, perhaps something else as well. Everything belonging to Kurtz had left my hands: soul, body, station, plans, ivory, career. Only his memory and his Intended remained. In a sense I wished to consign those too to the past, to deliver what I still held of him personally into the oblivion that concludes our shared fate. I make no defence. What I actually wanted was unclear even to me. Perhaps unconscious loyalty drove me, or one of those ironic obligations embedded in human existence. I do not know and cannot say. But I went.

“I supposed his memory resembled the other dead people’s memories accumulating through every life: a faint impression left in the mind by shadows falling upon it as they passed swiftly for the final time. Yet outside the heavy, tall doorway, between high houses in a street as quiet and proper as a cemetery’s carefully maintained avenue, I saw him again upon the stretcher. His mouth opened hungrily, as if to swallow the entire earth and every human being upon it. He lived before me, as fully alive as he had ever been: a shadow with an endless appetite for splendid appearances and dreadful realities, darker than night’s shadow, nobly clothed in the folds of gorgeous eloquence. The vision seemed to enter the house alongside me: stretcher, ghostly bearers, wild obedient worshippers, dark woods, the river’s glitter between shaded bends, the drum beating steadily and softly like a heart, the heart of victorious darkness. The wilderness seemed to triumph in a vengeful invasion that I alone must hold back to save another soul. I recalled what he had said far away out there, while horned figures moved behind me amid firelight and patient trees. Those broken phrases returned, audible again in all their ominous, terrifying simplicity. His abject pleading and abject threats, the immense proportions of his vile desires, his pettiness, suffering, the storm of anguish in his soul: I remembered it all. Then I saw his composed, languid manner another day: ‘This ivory really belongs to me. The Company never paid for it. I gathered it at enormous personal risk. Still, I fear they will claim it for themselves. H’m. A difficult matter. What should I do, do you think? Resist? Eh? I ask only for justice.’... Justice alone, nothing but justice. At the first-floor mahogany door I rang the bell. As I waited, he seemed to stare at me from its glass panel with that vast gaze embracing, condemning, loathing the whole universe. His whisper seemed audible again: ‘The horror! The horror!’

“Dusk was settling. I waited in a high drawing-room whose three floor-to-ceiling windows resembled luminous, draped columns. The furniture’s curved gilt legs and backs shone in blurred outlines. A tall white marble fireplace stood coldly monumental. In one corner a grand piano bulked like a polished, sombre sarcophagus, dark gleams crossing its flat surfaces. A tall door opened, then closed. I stood up.

“Dressed entirely in black, her pale head seemed to float towards me through the dimness. She wore mourning. More than a year had passed since his death and the arrival of the news, yet she looked prepared to remember and grieve eternally. Taking both my hands, she murmured, ‘I heard you were coming.’ She was not very young, I noticed, not girlish. Fidelity, belief, and suffering found a mature capacity in her. The room seemed darker, as though all the cloudy evening’s sorrowful light had gathered on her forehead. Fair hair, pale face, pure brow appeared within an ash-grey halo, out of which dark eyes looked at me with innocent depth, confidence, and trust. She carried her grieving head proudly, seeming to say, ‘I—I alone know how to mourn for him as he deserves.’ While we still clasped hands, however, a look of such terrible desolation crossed her face that I recognized someone Time could not toy with. To her his death was yesterday. By Jove! So powerful was the impression that it became yesterday for me too, indeed this very minute. I saw them at the same instant, his dying and her mourning, her grief within his moment of death. Can you understand? I saw and heard them together. Catching her breath deeply, she said, ‘I have survived,’ while through her despairing regret my straining ears distinctly heard the whisper that summed up his eternal condemnation. Panic stirred in my heart. What was I doing here, as if I had stumbled among cruel, absurd mysteries no human should witness? She indicated a chair, and we sat. Gently I set the packet on a little table. Her hand covered it.... After a mourning silence she whispered, ‘You knew him well.’
“‘People become close very quickly out there,’ I replied. ‘I knew him as completely as any man can ever know another.’
“‘You admired him too,’ she said. ‘Knowing him without admiring him would have been impossible, wouldn’t it?’
“‘He was an extraordinary man,’ I answered uncertainly. Her pleading, unwavering eyes seemed to wait upon my lips for further words, so I continued: ‘One could not help—’
“‘Loving him,’ she eagerly concluded, leaving me horrified and speechless. ‘How true! So true! And to think nobody knew him as I did! He shared all his noble thoughts with me. I understood him best.’
“‘You understood him best,’ I echoed. Perhaps she had. Yet each spoken word seemed to darken the room further. Only her smooth, white forehead stayed bright with the undying light of love and faith.

“‘You were his friend,’ she continued. ‘His friend,’ she said again, raising her voice slightly. ‘You must have been, since he entrusted this to you and sent you here. I feel able to speak to you, and oh! I need to speak. You heard his final words. I want you to know that I deserved him.... It is not pride.... Yes! I am proud that I understood him better than anyone living. He told me so himself. Since his mother’s death there has been nobody, nobody to—to—’

“I listened as the room grew darker. I was not certain he had even handed over the intended packet. I suspect he meant me to guard a different set of papers, which I later saw the manager inspecting under the lamp after his death. The girl went on talking, relieved by her certainty of my sympathy, talking as a thirsty man drinks. I had heard that her family opposed the engagement. Kurtz lacked sufficient money, or something similar. Indeed, for all I know he had lived in poverty always. Something he said suggested that impatience with relative poverty had driven him out there.

“‘... Who could hear him speak even once and fail to become his friend?’ she was saying. ‘He attracted people through whatever was best within them.’ Her eyes held mine intensely. ‘Great men possess that gift,’ she continued. Accompanying her quiet voice, I seemed to hear all the other sounds I had ever known that were full of mystery, desolation, and sorrow: water rippling, wind sighing through swaying trees, crowds murmuring, the faint ring of incomprehensible words shouted far away, a voice whispering from beyond the entrance to eternal darkness. ‘But you heard him yourself! You know!’ she cried.

“‘Yes, I know,’ I replied, feeling something close to despair. Yet I bowed my head before her faith, before that immense, saving illusion glowing unnaturally in the dark, the victorious darkness against which I could not have protected her, against which I could not protect even myself.

“‘Such a loss for me—for us!’ she corrected herself with lovely generosity, then softly added, ‘For the world.’ In twilight’s final gleams I could see her eyes shining with tears, tears that gathered there but would not fall.
“‘I was so happy, so fortunate, so proud,’ she continued. ‘Too fortunate, too happy, for that brief time. Now unhappiness will last me—for all my life.’
“She rose. Her fair hair gathered what light remained into a faint golden gleam. I stood as well.
“‘And of everything,’ she said sadly, ‘all that promise and greatness, his generous mind and noble heart, nothing survives except a memory. Nothing else. You and I—’
“‘We will never forget him,’ I hurriedly assured her.

“‘No!’ she exclaimed. ‘It cannot all vanish. Such a life cannot have been sacrificed to leave only grief. You knew the enormous plans he had. I knew them too, though perhaps I could not understand. Others knew. Something must survive. At least his words are still alive.’
“‘What he said will survive,’ I answered.
“‘His example too,’ she whispered, almost to herself. ‘People revered him. Everything he did revealed his goodness. That example—’
“‘Yes,’ I replied. ‘His example as well. Certainly, his example. I had forgotten.’
“‘I have not forgotten. I cannot believe it, cannot yet believe that I shall never see him again, that no one will ever see him again. Never, never, never.’

“She extended her arms as though reaching for someone drawing away, stretching them back with pale hands clasped across the window’s narrow, fading gleam. Never see him! At that instant I saw him plainly enough. Throughout my life that eloquent ghost will remain before me, and she will too: a familiar, tragic Shade whose gesture recalled another tragic figure, hung with useless charms, reaching bare brown arms over the glitter of that hellish river, that river of darkness. Suddenly she spoke very softly: ‘He died as he lived.’
“‘His death,’ I said, a dull resentment stirring within me, ‘was entirely fitting to the life he lived.’
“‘And I was not there beside him,’ she whispered. A feeling of boundless pity swept away my anger.
“‘We did all that was possible—’ I muttered.
“‘Ah, but nobody on earth believed in him as I did, not even his mother, not even he himself. He needed me! Me! I would have cherished each sigh and word, each movement, each look.’
“A cold hand seemed to tighten around my chest. ‘Please don’t,’ I said thickly.

“‘Forgive me. For so long I have grieved without speaking, without speaking.... You stayed beside him until the end? I imagine his loneliness. Nobody there to understand as I could have understood. Perhaps nobody even to listen....’
“‘Until the very end,’ I replied, my voice trembling. ‘I heard the last words he spoke....’ Fright made me stop.
“‘Tell me them,’ she whispered broken-heartedly. ‘I need—I need something, something I can—can live with.’

“I almost cried, ‘Can’t you hear them?’ Around us the dusk whispered them over and over. That whisper seemed to rise threateningly, like the first breath of an approaching wind. ‘The horror! The horror!’
“‘His final word, something to live with,’ she pleaded. ‘Do you not understand? I loved him, loved him, loved him!’
“Gathering my composure, I answered her slowly.
“‘Your name was the last word he spoke.’

“A soft sigh reached me. Then my heart seemed to stop, struck still by a terrible, exultant cry, an unimaginable triumph mingled with inexpressible pain. ‘I knew it—I was sure!’... She knew; she was certain. Hiding her face in her hands, she wept. I thought the house might fall before I escaped, the heavens collapse upon me. Nothing happened. Heaven does not fall over such a small matter. Would it have fallen, I wonder, had I given Kurtz the justice he deserved? Had he not asked only for justice? But I could not. I could not tell her the truth. It would have been too dark, altogether too dark....”

Marlow finished and remained apart from us, dim and silent, seated like a Buddha in meditation. For a while nobody stirred. Abruptly the Director said, ‘We have missed the beginning of the ebb.’ I looked up. A black mass of cloud blocked the seaward distance. Beneath the overcast sky the peaceful waterway, flowing towards the farthest ends of the earth, ran darkly on, seeming to lead into the heart of an immense darkness.
